NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Scan or Index? large Evidence Coverage, Answer Quality, and Cost in Long-Document RAG
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Scanning every passage in a long document seems thorough, but does it preserve more useful evidence or produce better answers? We compare 11 retrieval configurations spanning lexical and dense search, hybrid reranking, and full-document scanning with Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and Cloudflare Clef. Our evaluation uses 396 QASPER questions and 80 questions from eight complete textbooks, with common passages, a five-passage limit, and a fixed answer generator. On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), compared with 88.7% for Jev full scan and 81.3\% for OpenAI dense retrieval. Full scans examine every passage initially, yet later reduction steps can discard relevant evidence. Higher evidence coverage also does not consistently produce better answers: Hybrid + Decisions achieves the highest observed book Answer Accuracy among retrieval methods (0.892), despite recovering less reference evidence. Full scanning incurs substantially higher latency on books under the tested deployments, while reusable dense retrieval has lower projected API cost than paid decision-based methods as queries accumulate. Most QASPER articles already fit within the hybrid candidate pool, limiting the benefit of scanning. These results highlight evidence retention, answer quality, and reuse cost as complementary criteria for choosing a long-document retrieval strategy.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and training. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to changes affecting its scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce SANE, an agent-based framework that encodes behavioral requirements for stochastic evaluators as reusable agent instructions. Given a scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs, the pipeline first identifies scorer-specific capabilities, then automatically derives perturbation recipes and expected score relations for each. SANE also defines a scorer-independent validation framework for generated judge tests. It determines whether each recipe agrees with scorer intent and whether each instantiated case realizes the recipe and supports its expected relation. Because SANE generates a recipe inventory tailored to each scorer, the number of aligned recipes grows as scorers are added. Across five domains, SANE produces 3.7 times as many validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (JRH) at comparable end-to-end validity and detects scorer deficiencies in every domain, including professionalism and toxicity, where JRH detects none. On faithfulness, SANE achieves strong human alignment in judge ranking: its test-suite scores rank 11 judge models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance (Spearman rho = 0.852), while JRH does not (rho = 0.100).

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

Distributed Computing (Top Venues & Labs.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
Distributed Computing (Top Venues & Labs.summary: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP

Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).summary: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).title: ROAR: Benchmarking LMM Agents under Real-Time Constraints in Multiplayer Action-Shooter Games
Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Large multimodal models (LMMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that perceive, reason, and act in interactive multi-agent environments. Yet most existing benchmarks for LMM-based agents in multi-agent settings remain turn-based: the environment and other agents pause while an agent performs inference. Such protocols obscure a fundamental challenge of real-time constraints, where the world continues to evolve and delayed decisions may become outdated before execution. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce ROAR, a multiplayer action-shooter game environment for evaluating LMM-based agents in multi-agent settings under real-time constraints. ROAR covers cooperative, competitive, mixed cooperative-competitive, and basic single-agent scenarios. We further propose a Multi-Agent Asynchronous Gym interface that decouples environment evolution from agent reasoning by running the environment and each agent in separate threads, enabling the environment to advance at fixed time intervals without waiting for LMM inference and allowing agents to reason independently without blocking one another. ROAR also features convenient deployment, multimodal observations, and customizable levels. ROAR offers a practical testbed for advancing LMM-based agents beyond static, turn-based evaluation toward real-time multi-agent decision-making.

Databases (Core).title: Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models
Databases (Core).summary: Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.

Databases (Core).title: Building SQL Equivalence Proofs from Query Rewrite Rules
Databases (Core).summary: Query rewriting and semantic evaluation of text-to-SQL systems both depend on deciding whether two SQL queries return the same result on every database satisfying the schema constraints. Decades of equivalence-preserving optimizer rules provide a natural basis for constructive proofs: two queries are equivalent when admitted rewrites transform them to a common logical expression. Building on this observation, \sys{} organizes query-rewriting knowledge as a standalone proof-producing system. It separates rule validation from proof discovery, explicitly aligns alternative query representations, and returns the resulting rewrite derivation. Across three corpus classes, EquiTrace proves 648/1,106 expected-equivalent text-to-SQL pairs (58.6%), 229/266 curated pairs (86.1%), and 97/240 LLM-generated rewrites whose results agree under benchmark execution (40.4%). On the query rewrite corpus, EquiTrace proves 97 pairs, compared with 35 for QED and 38 for SQLSolver. An analysis of 1,242 recorded proofs shows that coverage depends on a small number of transformations, while many frequently used rules are individually substitutable. The resulting derivations make each proof replayable and expose the specific transformations on which it depends.

Databases (Core).title: Resilience for Regular Path Queries: Towards a Complexity Classification
Databases (Core).summary:
The resilience problem for a query and an input set or bag database is to compute the minimum number of facts to remove from the database to make the query false. In this paper, we study how to compute the resilience of Regular Path Queries (RPQs) over graph databases. Our goal is to characterize the regular languages L for which it is tractable to compute the resilience of the existentially-quantified RPQ built from L.
  We show that computing the resilience in this sense is tractable (even in combined complexity) for all RPQs defined from so-called local languages. By contrast, we show hardness in data complexity for RPQs defined from the following language classes (after reducing the languages to eliminate redundant words): all finite languages featuring a word containing a repeated letter, and all languages featuring a specific kind of counterexample to being local (which we call four-legged languages). The latter include in particular all languages that are not star-free. Our results also imply a dichotomy on all languages with a so-called neutral letter. We last show tractability for some classes of non-local languages, namely the so-called bipartite chain languages and one-dangling languages, and highlight some remaining obstacles towards a full dichotomy.

Databases (Core).title: Latent Bridges for Multi-Table Question Answering
Databases (Core).summary: We introduce GRAB, a constructor-encoder-bridge pipeline for table question answering. Our method lifts relational data into an heterogeneous graph, encodes it via message passing, and transfers the signals to an LLM through a small set of query-conditioned latent tokens. This provides the LLM with a compact, task-relevant structural representation together with the flattened text. Crucially, the LLM remains strictly frozen to preserve its general reasoning capabilities; we train only the lightweight graph encoder and latent bridge (91M parameters), allowing the entire pipeline to be trained efficiently. Our pipeline significantly improves performance on relational Question Answering, with the largest gains in demanding multi-table settings, offering an efficient, principled way to connect relational deep learning with LLMs.

Databases (Core).title: WaRP: Workload-Aware Request Planning for Vector Retrieval on Object Storage
Databases (Core).summary:
Modern vector search systems keep payload vectors in cloud object storage and only a compact routing index on fast local storage, typically using cluster-based ANN indexes. This design inherits a problem existing systems do not address. On object storage, small Range-GETs have latency dominated by fixed per-request overhead and are billed per request. Existing readers either issue one request per probed cluster, or coalesce adjacent ranges with hand-tuned gap or span thresholds that do not transfer across datasets or query workloads.
  We formulate the grouping of probed-cluster byte intervals into object-store requests as a global per-query optimization problem and present WaRP, a workload-aware request planner that solves it efficiently. Given the sorted byte intervals, a limit on the number of requests per query, and an estimate of how many object-store requests from one query can proceed concurrently under the target serving configuration, WaRP searches for a merge plan that minimizes a concurrency-aware latency surrogate while satisfying the request limit. Using an optimized dynamic program and adaptive frontier search, WaRP returns a plan within $(1{+}ε)$ of the optimum, with per-query planning overhead under $10$ms even in the most demanding tested settings. A lightweight offline reordering pass further improves request mergeability without changing the semantics of ANN search.
  We implement WaRP inside Lance's I/O scheduler and evaluate it on AWS S3. We build IVFPQ indexes on seven datasets, including SIFT100M and DEEP100M at the 100M-vector scale. WaRP + Reorder improves QPS by $1.09--3.48\times$ and reduces GETs by $2.12--5.19\times$ relative to Lance, while preserving Lance's recall.

Databases (Core).title: Conflicted Records: Typed Adversarial Contracts for Auditable LLM Output Quality Enforcement
Databases (Core).summary: LLM-generated records increasingly populate production information systems where they are treated as data assets subject to the same quality expectations as records from operational databases. A single such record can simultaneously satisfy and violate a quality rule: a grounded fact adjacent to a hallucination, a useful answer adjacent to a stereotype. Classical data cleaning cannot resolve this because the two judgments are incompatible over the same span; a single LLM judge cannot either, since it shares the training biases that produced the conflict. Existing interventions such as prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, and RLHF reduce surface error rates but provide no audit trail and cannot distinguish genuine remediation from blanket suppression. The question is whether a deterministic check over structured inter-agent records can catch the defects that referential checks alone miss. We present BiasGuard-D: two adversarial roles drawn from distinct model families exchange typed claim documents, a three-model quorum adjudicates by majority vote, and a combined referential-plus-semantic invariant validates the verdict. The semantic component fires on verdicts referential checks miss; removing the iterative loop drops invariant satisfaction sharply. The deliberation layer transfers from stereotype to hallucination remediation on HaluEval QA with only role-framing changes, raising right-answer recovery by 49 percentage points; the triage gate required a cross-family second auditor to maintain recall on objective hallucination. Every claim, vote, and instruction is stored as a typed record giving operators a provenance trail auditable under emerging AI regulations.

Databases (Core).title: Ozone: A Unified Platform for Transportation Research
Databases (Core).summary: Transportation research increasingly depends on heterogeneous data from roadside cameras, UAV imagery, LiDAR, and in-vehicle sensors. Differences in data representations, model interfaces, and evaluation protocols complicate cross-dataset benchmarking and reproducibility. We present Ozone, a unified transportation research platform organized around Hardware, Data, Model, and Evaluation layers, with a Prototype layer supporting deployment-oriented applications. Its data layer links vehicle trajectories, traffic conflicts, reconstructed crashes, and digital-twin maps through a shared trajectory schema. The source inventory spans 19 trajectory datasets recorded at 59 sites in eight countries, with completed converters for 12 sources and adaptation ongoing for seven. The converters align coordinate systems, object classes, oriented bounding boxes, and kinematic fields. A shared implementation of surrogate safety measures supports conflict extraction, while map and motion constraints link crash reports to reconstructed trajectories. CARLA digital-twin maps and SUMO traffic logic connect these records to simulation, model development, and evaluation. Validation on 500 vehicles from four datasets reports mean position, heading, and speed errors below 0.15 m, 2.5°, and 0.3 m/s. A workflow study reports an 85 % reduction in experiment setup time. Case studies demonstrate human-factor experiments and automated-driving safety testing, while the model interfaces support traffic modeling and world-model research. The source code and datasets are publicly available.

Databases (Core).title: NousDB - A Fast Query Engine for Semantic Analytics
Databases (Core).summary: Semantic data analytics systems integrate AI-powered operators into query pipelines, enabling declarative queries over structured and unstructured data. However, existing systems rely on per-tuple model invocations, ad hoc operator designs, and lack principled cost models, resulting in poor scalability and limited optimization. We present NousDB, a high-performance semantic analytics engine built on Apache DataFusion[22]. Through NousDB we propose an extended relational algebra with three semantic operators and formal algebraic properties that enable principled query rewriting and cross-operator optimization. We further propose a token-based cost model using equi-depth token histograms to optimize batch sizing under context-window constraints and provide statistical guarantees for safe batching. Experiments show that NousDB achieves up to x86 speedups with both local and enterprise LLMs, while leading competitors in token efficiency and accuracy. These gains extend to complex JOB and Stack workloads augmented with semantic operators, supporting both traditional and semantic analytics.

Databases (Core).title: Efficient Path Query Processing in Relational Database Systems
Databases (Core).summary: Path queries are crucial for property graphs, and there is growing interest in queries that combine regular expressions over labels with constraints on property values of vertices and edges. Efficient evaluation of such general path queries requires that intermediate results be eliminated early when there is no possible completion to a full result path. Neither state-of-the-art (SOA) graph DBMS nor relational DBMS currently can do this effectively for a large class of queries. We show that this problem can be addressed by giving a relational optimizer ``a little help'' by specifying early filtering opportunities explicitly in the query. To this end, we propose ReCAP, an abstraction that greatly simplifies the implementation of early filtering techniques for any type of property constraint for which such early filtering can be derived. No matter how complex the constraint, one only needs to implement (1) an NFA-style state transition function and (2) a handful of functions that mirror those needed for user-defined aggregates. We show that when using ReCAP, a standard relational DBMS like DuckDB can effectively push property constraints deep into the query plan, beating the SOA graph and relational DBMS by a factor up to 400,000 over a variety of queries and input graphs.

Databases (Core).title: LatentStore: An Efficient Latent-First Storage System for AI-Generated Images
Databases (Core).summary: The explosive growth of AI-generated images has created a sustainability challenge for storage infrastructure. Platforms like Midjourney and Adobe Firefly already host billions of generative images, yet conventional object stores persist them as blobs with full-resolution pixels, consuming huge amounts of storage capacity and bandwidth. Unlike natural photos, however, AI-generated images can be deterministically reconstructed from compact, model-native latent tensors, making persistent image storage fundamentally redundant. This paper presents LatentStore, a latent-first storage system for AI-generated images. LatentStore treats compressed latents as durable storage objects and uses on-demand GPU reconstruction on the read path to trade inexpensive compute for large persistent storage savings. Our design is guided by the first large-scale analysis of AI-generated image access we are aware of, based on a 35-month, 2-billion-request production trace from a major generative-content platform. Motivated by the trace analysis, LatentStore keeps frequently accessed images in decoded pixel format for fast hits, stores less-active objects as compressed latents to expand effective cache capacity, and continuously adjusts the splits between the image and latent cache to optimize user-perceived access latency. We build a LatentStore prototype and evaluate it with the production trace. LatentStore reduces persistent storage by 78.7% with competitive or even lower mean and tail latency over a pure image-based storage.

Databases (Core).title: Getting a GRIP on Graph-Based Search for Learned Sparse Retrieval
Databases (Core).summary: Learned sparse retrieval (LSR) has recently gained traction in the information retrieval community for the ability to combine the generalization capabilities of neural representations with the interpretability of keyword-based search. A number of recent works have demonstrated that inverted indexes, when appropriately modified for learned sparse embeddings, achieve state-of-the-art recall-latency tradeoffs for LSR, often outperforming graph-based indexes by substantial margins in latency at a fixed recall target. As a result, the community has generally concluded that graph-based approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search is inferior to inverted indexes for LSR. This paper challenges this conventional wisdom. Our key insight is that, while applying standard graph-based ANN indexes out-of-the-box to sparse vectors leads to uncompetitive performance, we can overcome these shortcomings by infusing the strengths of inverted indexes into graph-based search. In particular, we introduce three techniques to accelerate graph-based LSR: (i) term-based entry point seeding, (ii) approximate routing via sparse sketching, and (iii) sparse partition-based graph construction. We combine these techniques into a new graph-based ANN system for LSR we call GRIP. On the MS MARCO v2 benchmark (138M passages) with SPLADE embeddings, GRIP achieves a $2.5\times$ latency improvement over Seismic, a state-of-the-art inverted index tailored for LSR, at 95\% recall@10. Ultimately, our results call into question the default choice of inverted indexes for deploying learned sparse retrieval.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: SWE-DIVE: Multi-Turn Coding Agent Evaluation with Dynamic User Simulation
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary:
Coding agents are typically evaluated using one-shot, well-formulated prompts. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. However, in real-world use cases, prompts are often not as well-formulated or structured as existing GitHub issues. Additionally, a coding agent session is not limited to a single prompt; it typically involves a multi-turn interaction in which the user iteratively adds new tasks and requirements that the agent must fulfill.
  To benchmark these abilities, we developed SWE-DIVE, a dynamic, interactive validation and evaluation framework for benchmarking coding agents in a multi-turn environment. To achieve this, we introduce a user simulator that can simulate different behavioral patterns and communicate with the coding agent. We also introduce a conversation validator that evaluates the user simulator's outputs to determine whether they fulfill the initial requirements and guide the agent toward successfully solving the task. The entire framework is embedded in a Harbor environment, which orchestrates the coding agent, user simulator, and conversation validator, and executes the test environment to determine whether the agent successfully solves the task. Our results and source code are available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/swe-dive_usersim).

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: What the Author Wrote, What the Agent Reads: Silent Cue Loss in Enterprise Document Ingestion
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Enterprise agents act on documents. Before an agent can follow a policy, answer a compliance question or file a ticket, some ingestion layer must turn a Word file or PDF into tokens - and that layer is where an agent deployed in the wild silently loses information. We show that one layer is lost by every mainstream converter - the meaning an author encodes in how text looks - and that the loss makes agents confidently wrong rather than visibly incomplete. We build a task from 76 real policy documents: recover the requirements the author singled out, scored against the file's own OOXML properties by a deterministic matcher with no LLM judge. Formatting-blind ingestion collapses from micro F1 0.690 to 0.150 (docling) and 0.075 (plain text), a gap that replicates across six answering models from two vendors - five Claude models spanning the Opus, Sonnet and Haiku tiers, and OpenAI's GPT-5.6. An agent that cannot see the cue guesses, and docling's false-positive rate on requirements the author did not flag is four times ours. A span-level leave-one-out localises the loss to two cues - highlight (+0.302) and colour (+0.262), both Holm-adjusted p < 1e-4 - while bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough each sit within +/-0.003 of zero. The same asymmetry appears in PDF. Colour is also the cue no mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores, and it is common: 32.8% of 6,460 documents carry a deliberate colour or highlight, 10.3% on an obligation. A pre-registered test shows that typing a cue for the agent adds +0.085 beyond merely preserving it (Holm-adjusted p = 0.049). We validate the labels against rendered page images through an independent modality (kappa = 0.72) and bound what wording alone can achieve (AUC 0.664). For agent builders the practical finding is that ingestion, not reasoning, is where this reliability is won or lost, and that the fix is cheap and measurable.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: One-Slide Calibration of Pathology Foundation Models
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Scanner variation changes how pathology foundation models represent the same tissue. We introduce SlideRuler, which uses other regions within a slide as internal controls to predict a query region's scanner-induced shift. A transfer map learned from paired rescans enables calibration from a single scan at inference while keeping the foundation model fixed. Across two encoders and five SCORPION scanners, learned transfer reduces mean target-to-source embedding distance by 16.3-38.5% relative to raw embeddings. Replacing controls with unrelated same-scanner regions reveals a positive same-slide contribution in all four evaluation settings, including scanner holdout. A source-anchored variant reduces source-feature displacement by 47.7-83.6% relative to learned transfer while retaining most of its alignment gain. By drawing calibration information from the slide itself, SlideRuler offers a path toward more consistent use of frozen pathology models across imaging systems.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: On the Expressive Power and Limitations of Multi-Layer SSMs
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: We study how depth, finite precision, state dimension, and chain-of-thought (CoT) affect the expressive power of multi-layer state-space models (SSMs). For the explicit-table $K$-function-composition problem, a canonical benchmark for sequential information propagation, we prove that any $L$-layer SSM solving $(L+3)$-function composition must satisfy $d^2p=Ω(N/L^3)$, where $d$ is the state dimension and $p$ is the per-scalar precision. Conversely, $K$-function composition is solved exactly by a $(K+1)$-layer generalized SSM with $d=1$ and $p=Θ(\log N)$. This gives a worst-case depth hierarchy for this formal problem family. We then distinguish post-input reasoning, in which all thought tokens are generated after the input, from input-interleaved reasoning, in which thought tokens may be inserted while the input stream is being read. Post-input reasoning does not circumvent our communication-based lower-bound pipeline, whereas input-interleaved reasoning admits bidirectional simulations with general deterministic one-pass streaming algorithms at the granularity of persistent memory. Finally, width and precision are not interchangeable under exact step-preserving simulation in the base affine-state model, but become interchangeable through the streaming-memory characterization once input-interleaved reasoning is allowed.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring offers actionable evidence for oversight AI systems, with the potential to enable early detection and intervention. However, existing approaches are focused on specific tasks, whereas the regulation of AI, particularly reasoning models, requires monitoring a broader range of tasks. We introduce Factor for CoT monitoring, a strategy that supports customizing monitoring requirements in the prompt, which enables a single monitor to cover different tasks by relying on different factors. Furthermore, we introduce two types of factors, fine-grained and coarse-grained (e.g., monitoring whether a specific email address has been leaked versus monitoring privacy leakage), to accommodate diverse user monitoring needs. Based on this, we develop a CoT monitor named OwlSight that relies solely on factor to monitor behaviors related to multiple dimensions, including capability, safety, and trustworthiness. Experiments across 15,971 reasoning trajectories show that OwlSight surpasses general-purpose LLMs by 1.32-30.57 and 11.71-27.81 points at fine and coarse granularity, respectively, and achieves state-of-the-art results on OpenAI's CoT monitorability benchmark. It also generalizes to unseen models' CoTs and remains robust to Factor rephrasings, CoT compression, and obfuscation, offering a promising paradigm for CoT monitoring that can contribute to the oversight of frontier AI.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Brittlebench: Quantifying LLM robustness via prompt sensitivity
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Existing evaluation methods largely rely on clean, static benchmarks, which can overestimate true model performance by failing to capture the noise and variability inherent in real-world user inputs. This is especially true for language models, which can face human-generated text queries containing mistakes, typos, or alternative ways of phrasing the same question. In this work, we introduce a theoretical framework for quantifying model sensitivity to prompt variants, or brittleness, that can enable us to disentangle data-induced difficulty from prompt-related variability. Using this framework, we design a novel evaluation pipeline, Brittlebench, to holistically evaluate the sensitivity of frontier models. We apply semantics-preserving perturbations to a suite of popular benchmarks, and observe model performance to degrade as much as 12%. However, these perturbations do not affect all models equally: even a single perturbation alters the relative ranking of models in 63% of cases, impacting conclusions about comparative model performance. Decomposing the total variance of both state-of-the-art open-weight and commercial models, we find that semantics-preserving input perturbations can account for up to half of the performance variance for a given model. Brittlebench highlights the need for more robust evaluations and models, and allows us to systematically understand model brittleness.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Behind Aggregate Scores: What Systematically Varying Arena-Hard's LLM Judge Reveals
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: LLM judges are used to determine which of two answers is better. Trusting these verdicts requires knowing how repeatable they are and how much they depend on the judge's instructions. We show that similar aggregate scores can conceal substantial changes in individual verdicts, both when the same setup is repeated and when the instructions change. Using 500 Arena-Hard v2.0 prompts with two models' answers held fixed, we run GPT-4.1 as the judge under all eight combinations of criteria, output format and task framing, and repeat every setup unchanged at temperature zero on a pinned model version. Rerunning the default setup moves the aggregate score by about one point but changes the win/tie/loss outcome on 21.2% of prompts. Instruction changes introduce further sensitivity: in one setup, which asks for the verdict without reasoning and also drops several other instructions, outcomes change on 28.2 percentage points more prompts than the two setups' unchanged reruns do on average, and the aggregate score falls by 4.09 points. In another, where the criteria prioritise accuracy, outcomes change on 6.7 percentage points more prompts by the same comparison, while the aggregate score barely moves. A stable aggregate score therefore does not establish that individual verdicts are repeatable. This distinction matters when those verdicts are used as preference labels or to assess individual responses. Evaluations that rely on individual verdicts should repeat each setup they use and report both aggregate scores and prompt-level agreement.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Externalise the Memory: A Pre-Registered Study of Where an Embodied Agent's Experience Should Live
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision-conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre-registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p-value. Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an action-only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw - rather than refute - the memory-in-weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation-specific correction that retrieval supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19-26% to 53-55% (sensitivity 17-21% to 50-55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [-4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were originally motivated by discovering monosemantic features, a property that characterizes individual features but does not specify what the learned feature set should look like as a whole. As SAEs have increasingly been adopted for attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention, researchers have begun evaluating metrics that describe global properties of the feature set, such as sparsity, dead feature rates, reconstruction fidelity, and disentanglement, a diverse set that extends far beyond monosemanticity. However, this implicit shift beyond monosemanticity has not been formalized as a clear, well-defined objective that comes before these evaluation metrics. Without such an objective, existing metrics remain ad hoc, with their necessity unjustified. In this work, we formalize this ultimate objective by introducing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation: requiring that SAE features, and more generally dictionary-based decompositions of model representations, form an atomic interpretable unit basis, a coordinate system for semantically meaningful explanation. Under this paradigm, we organize existing and new measurements such as DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) as proxy metrics and introduce a comprehensive benchmarking framework. Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant. These failure modes warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training and architectures, and motivate dominance-aware evaluation as a standard check for practitioners before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous-research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but are limited by short fixed templates, low executability, and weak traceability, and none has been demonstrated end-to-end in a live computer-vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. Five design choices distinguish it: (i) candidates mutate plugins from a verified-reproduction backbone matched to published baselines; (ii) a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands scores candidates on measured GPU PSNR with verbal-gradient feedback; (iii) a standing falsifier subtracts Elo on failure, integrating stress-test survival into selection; (iv) every reported number is bound to a logged training run, and the run cannot terminate while any claim is unbacked; (v) a seven-category 3DGS taxonomy wraps EVOLVE-BLOCK markers in domain-aligned scaffolds transferable across 3DGS repositories. On PSNR-targeted runs, SplatLab's manuscripts beat their reproduced targets by +0.18 to +3.78 dB, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, for which no prior 3DGS method exists. The research cycle compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute. Code, all manuscripts, experiment ledgers, and the cross-run paper store are available on the project page.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Kernel-Managed Shared Memory for System-Wide Personalization
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: AI systems become more useful when they can adapt to the people using them, but in multi-agent systems, useful context learned by one agent often remains unavailable to others. We present kernel-managed shared memory, a system-level abstraction in which specialized agents write structured, tagged memories while the agent-system kernel, not individual agents, governs retrieval, privacy enforcement, and prompt injection. We implement and evaluate this design on AIOS and compare it against three alternatives across three assistant models (GPT-4o, Llama-3.1:8B, Qwen-2.5:7B) and 1,800 total trials. Against an unmanaged external memory backend (Mem0) using identical underlying storage, kernel-managed retrieval and injection improve personalization scores by 2.4-4.0 points on a 5-point scale (e.g., 1.05 to 4.69 profile usage on GPT-4o), with every comparison significant at p < 10^-18. Against standard retrieval-augmented injection, gains are similarly large and consistent across all three models. Against full, unfiltered context concatenation, a soft ceiling on available context rather than on response quality, kernel-managed injection statistically matches performance on two of three models and shows a small, model-specific deficit on the third, while using substantially shorter prompts: end-to-end latency is 15-61% lower across all three models, with corresponding reductions in per-call token usage and inference cost. These results indicate that centralizing memory management in the agent-system kernel, rather than leaving retrieval and privacy enforcement to individual agents, delivers most of the personalization benefit of unconstrained context at a fraction of its cost.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: FlashBoB: I/O-Efficient Exact Backward-over-Backward for Softmax Attention
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Transformer models built on the attention mechanism have become a central building block in modern deep learning, yet softmax attention remains a major bottleneck for long-context workloads. While FlashAttention makes the forward and first backward passes I/O-efficient, it does not support backward-over-backward (BoB), which enables exact differentiation through the backward pass for applications such as second-order optimization, test-time training, gradient-based memory, and meta-learning. Existing BoB implementations either materialize large intermediate tensors or exhaust GPU memory at long sequence lengths. We present FlashBoB, an exact, I/O-efficient algorithm for BoB in softmax attention that keeps computation within on-chip tiles and avoids all $N \times N$ intermediate tensors, where $N$ is the sequence length. The key insight is a hierarchical affine structure in the softmax double backward: two row-wise scalars determine all outputs through affine transformations. This yields a two-pass schedule with bounded on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM) usage and minimal off-chip high-bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic. FlashBoB achieves $Θ(N^2 d^2/M)$ HBM traffic ($d$ is the head dimension and $M$ is the memory size) and, within the standard FlashAttention-style score-recomputation model, matches the inherited large-cache lower bound for exact forward attention. Empirically, it scales exact attention BoB to $N=262\text{K}$ on a single A100 80GB GPU, where prior PyTorch exact baselines fail by $N=16\text{K}$, and is up to $6.3\times$ faster than FlashBack. These results make exact second-order attention practical at long-context sequence lengths where prior implementations cannot run efficiently.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Agent Mosaic: Recognizing Confidentiality Leaks in Agentic LLM Systems
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Modern LLM agents can retrieve information from accessible documents, and then disclose a sensitive conclusion assembled from them. This mosaic effect creates a critical risk for agents operating over confidential data. We quantify its realization with 30 synthetic cybersecurity, medical, and military examples, yielding 10,800 final answers from three LLM agents in controlled simulation and 1,440 answers from live agents in two open-source harnesses. Even under benign queries designed to be answerable from one document, GPT-5.6-Sol, the best performing model tested, discloses forbidden composites in 7.08% of answers (95% CI: 3.75-10.67%) in simulation, with worse disclosure rates in live harnesses. Adding visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules reduces pooled disclosure rates substantially, yet unsafe disclosures persist in 32.37% of simulated answers (95% CI: 28.33-36.19%) across all intents despite these safeguards. Furthermore, increased refusals do not guarantee confidentiality, since significant refusals reveal the prohibited conclusion regardless. These results point to a troubling conclusion: sensitive data leaks via mosaic-style events are an observed confidentiality failure mode in the evaluated settings at non-negligible rates. They motivate stronger controls on what agents may infer and disclose in sensitive data environments with mixed-clearance users.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: MemMux: Runtime Verification and Honest Resource Attribution for Fleets of Parallel Coding Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Developers increasingly run a fleet of coding agents side by side on one workstation. Terminal multiplexers like tmux and a new generation of agent managers were built to arrange windows, not to govern memory. When ten agents each spawn language servers, test runners, and browsers, no standard tool can say how much memory belongs to which agent, confirm that a terminated agent's descendants are gone, notice a child that has escaped its agent, or keep the machine off the swap cliff when an out-of-memory (OOM) kill would silently discard uncommitted work. We treat these as runtime-verification problems: a hosting substrate should emit signals an operator can check while agents run. We present MemMux, an unprivileged local runtime (no kernel control groups) turning resource governance into checkable signals: per-agent attribution, complete reclamation, escaped-process visibility, bounded footprint under overcommit, and monitoring overhead. A claims-disciplined benchmark measures each against tmux and a raw-process baseline on identical workloads. Under a binding memory budget on a Linux host, MemMux holds the fleet under budget (7500 MiB) with zero swap by admitting a subset and reclaiming under pressure, while the ungoverned tools run every agent, pin the machine at its RAM ceiling (2x over budget), and spill about 2 GiB into swap. MemMux reclaims 100% of a terminated agent's process subtree where the raw baseline strands half of it (tmux matches us here; the raw baseline does not), and it is the only launcher we compare against that surfaces escaped children (10 of 10 detected). The cost: the always-on 1 Hz monitoring loop runs near 0.6% CPU at one agent but 2.7% at ten, above our 2% target. Running the harness on real Claude Code sessions shows 100% attribution and low overhead carry over to live agent trees. We release the engine, benchmark, and reproducer.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: How Far Will They Go? Red-Teaming Online Influence with Large Language Models
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: As large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly participate in online discourse, red-teaming their capacity to support political influence campaigns is critical for information integrity. In pursuit of this goal, we focus on locally deployable open-source LLMs under an assumed threat model in which an operator seeks to avoid detection, prioritizes throughput, and selects released LLM checkpoints without modifying their weights. We introduce an empirical red-teaming framework for measuring LLM Overton Windows (OWs), summarizing expression fidelity across sampled political opinions, and for quantifying how simple natural-language jailbreaks change these scores. We evaluate more than 30 LLMs spanning 10 model families and five countries of origin on English-language, US-focused target opinions. We find systematic asymmetries in political expressivity: models typically express sampled left-leaning content with higher fidelity, mean OW scores tend to decrease with model size, and average expression fidelity varies across countries of origin in our sample. Jailbreak potency also varies sharply across model families, motivating a workflow for identifying effective combinations of jailbreak techniques. Our framework supports audits of political steerability and future countermeasure research.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Semantic Optimal Transport for Sparse Autoencoder Feature Matching and Circuit Compression
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a central tool for interpreting language models. However, two key SAE analyses that remain difficult to scale are (1) matching semantically similar features across multi-layers and (2) compressing large feature circuits into interpretable supernodes. Although these have been treated as separate problems, we show that both are instances of a more fundamental challenge, which we frame as the estimation of semantic distances between SAE features that lie on different activation manifolds. We introduce a distributional framework for this problem, in which each feature is represented not by a single decoder vector like in the literature, but by an activation-weighted distribution over the hidden states that express it. By projecting these distributions into a shared reference space and comparing them with Wasserstein distance, our method provides a unified semantic metric for cross-layer feature comparison. We prove that our representation is invariant to activation rescaling, stable under perturbations, and recovers true matches under finite-sample margin conditions. Empirically, our method outperforms decoder-vector and LLM-based baselines and captures subtle functional distinctions between related features. Notably, our method compresses large feature circuits into interpretable supernodes automatically.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: MemPlan: Memory-Conditioned PDDL Planning for Partially Observable Text Environments
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: LLM agents are flexible in language interaction, but using them as long-horizon planners is costly and prone to hallucinated or invalid actions. This paper targets a different role for LLMs: constrained bridges between language and symbolic planning. We propose MemPlan, a memory-conditioned PDDL planning framework for partially observable interactive text environments. MemPlan keeps the PDDL domain fixed and reconstructs the PDDL problem at each step from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns relevance-based action costs to candidate hypotheses for missing objects, locations, or conditions, guiding the planner toward more plausible checks. Negative memory records execution-refuted assumptions and compiles them into exclusion constraints, preventing repeated attempts at candidates already contradicted by feedback. A unified schema-conditioned language--symbol interface, trained offline with supervised fine-tuning, connects text environments to the planning loop through observation-to-fact parsing and symbolic-action-to-command grounding. Experiments on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille show that MemPlan improves task completion and step efficiency over language-only and PDDL-aware baselines, while substantially reducing online token cost compared with LLM-planning baselines such as ReAct. The same fine-tuned interface is also reused across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/tewiSong/MemPlan.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity efficiently by activating a small subset of parameters per token. However, in long-context inference, memory remains a major bottleneck because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce this cost for dense transformers, but overlook a problem specific to MoE: KV eviction can change which experts are selected during answer generation, degrading the generation quality. We propose MoEZip, a routing-aware KV cache compression for sparse MoE language models. To estimate the sensitivity of expert routing to perturbation, we propose a novel metric based on the Fisher information matrix of routing distributions. MoEZip combines this metric with attention weights for routing-aware scoring of contexts. Finally, we compose a complementary scoring system that combines eviction methods for dense and sparse-MoE architectures. Experiments show that MoEZip achieves robust performance under aggressive cache compression on various benchmarks. At a KV retention ratio of 10\%, MoEZip improves over the SoTA baseline by +24 and +20 points on average on LongBench and RULER, corresponding to 2.3$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ higher scores, respectively.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Velocity Ambiguity Profiles: Time-Resolved Bayes-Risk Diagnostics for Flow Matching
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Flow matching trains a continuum of velocity regression problems but usually reports a loss averaged over interpolation time, obscuring which regions are limited by intrinsic ambiguity and which remain data-limited. We introduce the Velocity Ambiguity Profile (VAP), $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$, the time-local Bayes-risk floor of velocity prediction, and decompose time-resolved loss as $L_N(t)=\mathcal{A}_v(t)+R(t;N)$, where only the excess term $R(t;N)$ is reducible by more data or a different estimator. For $N$ training samples and a $K$-component mixture in the structured example, we prove two statistical benchmarks. In an intrinsic local-regression benchmark, $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$ enters the time-dependent noise factor of the standard nonparametric rate. In separated isotropic Gaussian mixtures, the Bayes velocity becomes locally affine, and a label-oracle residual-regression benchmark has parametric excess-risk scale $K\mathcal{A}_v(t)/N$, matched within the same separated residual Gaussian-location subproblem. Controlled Gaussian-mixture experiments validate this diagnostic through a dense transition sweep, calibrated oracle-to-blind and empirical-proxy audits, and a local controlled time-sampler stress test in which a frozen reducible-error proxy reduces reducible loss while cross-cell sensitivity delimits aggressive sampling. On CIFAR-100 DINOv2 feature flow, guided time sampling reduces uniformly evaluated velocity loss by $6.78\%$ and global feature Fréchet distance (FD) by $23.6\%$, while class-conditional kernel inception distance (KID) shows no improvement. VAP turns an averaged flow-matching objective into a time-resolved diagnostic for locating ambiguity-limited and data-limited regions.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Training generative models on synthetic data causes loss of diversity and a decrease in performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. We study this degeneration spectrally in a controlled Markov setting. The eigenvalue spectrum of the learned transition operator offers a direct view of the process, since the subdominant eigenvalues set how fast the chain mixes and therefore how much of the state space it continues to explore. We find that sampling at temperature $T_s < 1$ acts on the operator like repeated sharpening, pushing it toward a deterministic system: the subdominant eigenvalues approach the unit circle and the spectral gap narrows. When $T_s < 1$, even data accumulation does not appear to arrest this drift. We then analyze Dreaming Learning, a regulariser that, in parallel with regular training, adds a loss term on the model's own samples drawn at a raised temperature $T_d > 1$. Because high-temperature samples flatten the predicted distribution, training on them keeps the entries of the learned operator from becoming vanishingly small, which in turn keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle. Measurements of the spectra over 5000 generations are consistent with this picture, and the mitigation effect persists in more complex settings such as LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: SCDM: Scalable Causal Discovery in Nonlinear Temporal Systems with Meta-Learning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Causal discovery from nonlinear multivariate time series is challenging in high-dimensional systems, where the number of candidate directed relations grows quadratically with the number of variables. Existing methods are often limited by target-wise model fitting, repeated conditional testing, or expensive graph-search procedures. We propose SCDM, a shared-parameter meta-learning framework for scalable temporal causal discovery. SCDM treats each target variable as a task while learning a shared temporal predictor and a shared causal-strength matrix across tasks. Each meta-episode updates only a subset of target-variable tasks, allowing the model to accumulate structural evidence across the full system without exhaustive target-wise optimization. After training, a post-training graph readout converts the learned predictor into continuous directed causal scores for threshold-independent evaluation. We also provide a finite-error recovery principle showing that, under fully observed delayed-system assumptions and a positive risk-gap condition, thresholding SCDM scores recovers the graph when statistical, meta-optimization, and readout errors are below the population margin. Experiments on controlled synthetic, neuroimaging-inspired, high-dimensional, and real-world temporal benchmarks demonstrate competitive causal recovery and improved scalability in large temporal systems.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: On the Expressive Power and Limitations of Multi-Layer SSMs
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: We study how depth, finite precision, state dimension, and chain-of-thought (CoT) affect the expressive power of multi-layer state-space models (SSMs). For the explicit-table $K$-function-composition problem, a canonical benchmark for sequential information propagation, we prove that any $L$-layer SSM solving $(L+3)$-function composition must satisfy $d^2p=Ω(N/L^3)$, where $d$ is the state dimension and $p$ is the per-scalar precision. Conversely, $K$-function composition is solved exactly by a $(K+1)$-layer generalized SSM with $d=1$ and $p=Θ(\log N)$. This gives a worst-case depth hierarchy for this formal problem family. We then distinguish post-input reasoning, in which all thought tokens are generated after the input, from input-interleaved reasoning, in which thought tokens may be inserted while the input stream is being read. Post-input reasoning does not circumvent our communication-based lower-bound pipeline, whereas input-interleaved reasoning admits bidirectional simulations with general deterministic one-pass streaming algorithms at the granularity of persistent memory. Finally, width and precision are not interchangeable under exact step-preserving simulation in the base affine-state model, but become interchangeable through the streaming-memory characterization once input-interleaved reasoning is allowed.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: A Generalisation Signal Need Not Be a Model-Selection Signal
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Model selection in computational biology often relies on validation data drawn from the training regime, even when deployment lies outside it. When validation no longer preserves which model is best, a natural alternative is to rank candidates using properties of the trained network itself. We test this idea using a novel, forward-only proxy motivated by the norm of the Hessian, alongside common Hessian measures, across molecular property, protein fitness, and drug-response tasks. Contrary to our hypothesis, geometry does not become more useful as validation Spearman correlation deteriorates: augmenting validation helps some shifts but significantly harms others. More surprisingly, the proxy still correlates with generalisation gap on most tasks even when Hessian trace and top-eigenvalue relationships are weak or reversed, yet this signal does not reliably identify the deployment-best model. A curvature bound need not preserve cross-model rankings, and low geometric scores can even favour collapsed predictors. Thus, a generalisation signal need not be a model-selection signal.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: RubRIX: Rubric-Driven Risk Mitigation in Caregiver-AI Interactions
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Caregivers seeking AI-mediated support express complex needs---information-seeking, emotional validation, and distress cues---that warrant careful evaluation of response safety and appropriateness. Existing AI evaluation frameworks, primarily focused on general risks (toxicity, hallucinations, policy violations, etc), may not adequately capture the nuanced risks of LLM-responses in caregiving-contexts. We introduce RubRIX (Rubric-based Risk Index), a theory-driven, clinician-validated framework for evaluating risks in LLM caregiving responses. Grounded in the Elements of an Ethic of Care, RubRIX operationalizes five empirically-derived risk dimensions: Inattention, Bias & Stigma, Information Inaccuracy, Uncritical Affirmation, and Epistemic Arrogance. We evaluate six state-of-the-art LLMs on over 20,000 caregiver queries from Reddit and ALZConnected. Rubric-guided refinement consistently reduced risk-components by 45-98% after one iteration across models. This work contributes a methodological approach for developing domain-sensitive, user-centered evaluation frameworks for high-burden contexts. Our findings highlight the importance of domain-sensitive, interactional risk evaluation for the responsible deployment of LLMs in caregiving support contexts. We release benchmark datasets to enable future research on contextual risk evaluation in AI-mediated support.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.
