Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.title: Good Scores, Bad Data: A Metric for Multimodal Coherence
Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.summary: Multimodal AI systems are evaluated by downstream task accuracy, but high accuracy does not mean the underlying data is coherent. A model can score well on Visual Question Answering (VQA) while its inputs contradict each other. We introduce the Multimodal Coherence Score (MCS), a metric that evaluates fusion quality independent of any downstream model. MCS decomposes coherence into four dimensions, identity, spatial, semantic, and decision, with weights learned via Nelder-Mead optimization. We evaluate on 1,000 Visual Genome images using DETR, CLIP, and ViLT, and validate on 150 COCO images with no retraining. Across three fusion architectures, MCS discriminates quality with higher sensitivity than task accuracy alone (Spearman rho = 0.093 vs. 0.071). Perturbation experiments confirm each dimension responds independently to its failure mode with zero cross-talk. MCS is lightweight, requires no human annotation, and tells you not just that something broke, but what broke.

Distributed Computing (Top Venues & Labs.title: Speeding up Log-Sum-Exp: Kernel Fusion at the Memory Wall, Integer Arithmetic at the Compute Wall
Distributed Computing (Top Venues & Labs.summary: While the Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) function is a foundational numerical primitive for stable log-domain computation in modern machine learning, its fast and efficient computation on generic platforms (\ie, CPUs and GPUs) has been underexplored, potentially creating execution bottlenecks for large workloads. On GPU, the de facto implementation torch.logsumexp dispatches a chain of nine sub-kernels per call, incurring redundant High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) traffic and launch overhead. On CPU, exp and log operations are hardware-hungry, limiting the computing efficiency. To address these bottlenecks, we propose two drop-in kernels to significantly accelerate LSE computation on both GPUs and CPUs: FuseLSE, a single-pass fused kernel that evaluates LSE's exp and log functions on the GPU's Special Function Unit (SFU); and IntLSE, which further replaces the LSE computation with approximated integer arithmetic for CPU computation. Our experiments, validated by benchmarks across workload sizes and hardware platforms, show that both kernels are ${\sim}10-11\times$ faster than PyTorch at small workloads and ${\sim}6\times$ faster on larger ones on GPUs, where the speed-up is attributed to reduced launch overhead and HBM traffic. On CPU, where no SFU is available, LSE computation dominates the cost, allowing IntLSE to gain ${\sim}3-6\times$ execution speed over FuseLSE.

Databases (Core).title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution
Databases (Core).summary:
Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations.
  A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral.
  The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.

Databases (Core).title: Fast Approximate Line Nearest Neighbor Search
Databases (Core).summary: Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search, which retrieves vectors close to a given query vector, is a fundamental operation in vector databases. However, emerging applications, such as selecting source images for photo-based animation and video synthesis, may require matching content while allowing a query-specified aspect contrast, such as an illumination change, to vary; a single query point does not directly express this requirement. In this paper, we study approximate line nearest neighbor (LANN) search, where an infinite query line removes the distance contribution along a specified direction while database records remain points. Prior approaches focus on top-$1$ search only for LANN and can incur high construction costs. Converting LANN into ordinary point ANN search through dimension lifting substantially increases index construction and query costs, while direct search on a proximity graph built for ordinary point ANN search can miss distinct regions close to a line. To address these issues, we propose LinePG, which enhances an existing proximity graph with pair edges to facilitate navigation between separated near-line regions. To find these pair edges efficiently, we first generate region pairs with spatial or graph separation, and near a line. We then score edges between the selected region pairs to guide the point endpoint selections. We conduct extensive performance studies and confirm the accuracy and efficiency of LinePG in comparison with the baseline approaches.

Databases (Core).title: GraphRAGProv: GraphRAG Meets How-Provenance
Databases (Core).summary: GraphRAG systems often use knowledge graphs to retrieve relevant context for an LLM that produces the final answer. That makes answers more inscrutable and therefore less appealing for domains where transparency is paramount. We present GraphRAGProv, an architecture that executes SPARQL queries over source-grounded RDF graphs to compute answers and their how-provenance polynomials. These polynomials record which statement occurrences were used and how they were combined. Because each occurrence is linked to its source text, users can follow these links to check whether the extracted statements reflect the text and whether the query combines them to answer the question. Querying thereby becomes a way to inspect and evaluate the text-to-graph transformation. Our interactive demo examines 400 cases from two multi-hop QA benchmarks, revealing extraction and query errors even when the final answer is correct.

Databases (Core).title: Synthetic Hospital: An Open, Verifiable, Physician-Validated Longitudinal EHR Benchmark
Databases (Core).summary: Frontier language models are rarely used in clinical workflows because the realistic, longitudinal benchmarks needed to develop them are scarce. Real electronic health record (EHR) data cannot be openly shared due to privacy, ethics or data use issues and it does not contain verifiable ground truth since the chart records only reflect what clinicians documented. We introduce Synthetic Hospital, an open, fully synthetic, fact-grounded longitudinal EHR benchmark that resolves the open sharing and verifiable ground truth barriers. Built entirely from public medical-education material with no protected health information, it comprises 1,268 longitudinal patients and 5,602 encounters, where every diagnosis, finding, and temporal relation is grounded in standard ontologies (ICD-10-CM, SNOMED CT, LOINC) and with a complete provenance chain back to its source medical education material. Synthetic Hospital is served through a simulated hospital record system that mirrors real EHR infrastructure (standard interoperability APIs, role-based access and function-calling interface). In a blinded review, physicians distinguished its records from real patient charts at near-chance rates (53%). Across 10 frontier and open models, none approaches ceiling: the best model reconstructs a patient's longitudinal problem list with a severity-weighted F1 of 0.73, level with the mean of seven physicians on a matched subset but well below the best of them (0.89), and misses roughly half of clinically relevant findings when summarizing a chart. Overall, these results highlight that Synthetic Hospital is a difficult and realistic test of clinical AI performance.

Databases (Core).title: Hypergraph-Enhanced Evidence Selection for Long-Context Multimodal Document QA
Databases (Core).summary: Long-context multimodal document question answering (QA) has become an important yet challenging task for modern vision-language models (VLMs), as it requires reasoning over evidence dispersed across pages and modalities within limited input budgets. Current pipelines adopt retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to select multimodal evidence for downstream VLMs. However, existing systems mainly rely on static selection rules over fixed-granularity retrieval units such as pages or blocks, resulting in information loss during retrieval and suboptimal performance in downstream reasoning. To alleviate these issues, we formulate the core task as budget-aware evidence selection over structured document evidence and propose HyperDoc, a document RAG framework that constructs compact yet sufficient evidence while preserving document relations. Specifically, HyperDoc constructs a document hypergraph to explicitly capture structural, logical, and cross-modal relationships among multimodal document elements. Over this structured evidence space, HyperDoc performs adaptive cost-aware hyperedge selection based on query intent and input budget. Extensive experiments on three representative benchmarks demonstrate that HyperDoc outperforms various types of state-of-the-art baselines.

Databases (Core).title: Back to the Future: The Evolving Universal Relation Model
Databases (Core).summary: Document backed analytics need databases that can be built as queries arrive. Enterprises increasingly ask analytical queries over messy document collections such as contracts, invoices, reports, emails, policies, and tickets, where the relevant structure and facts are often not known in advance. RAG can retrieve and summarize supporting evidence, but it does not by itself produce reusable, joinable, governed database state. Schema first construction offers the opposite strength: once a database is built, it supports joins, aggregation, constraints, indexes, optimization, and transactions. Yet for document analytics, fixing the schema and extracting all possible fields upfront is both expensive and brittle, because later queries and new documents often surface concepts that were not modeled before. We propose the Evolving Universal Relation Model (EUR), a query first model for document backed analytics. Users ask natural language queries as if the document corpus exposed one conceptual relation over application concepts. Internally, the DBMS turns each query into controlled database evolution: it updates the logical schema when new concepts are needed, extracts and integrates the facts required to answer the query, and decides what durable database state should remain for future queries. Thus, in EUR, a query is not only evaluated; it also helps construct the database. Document backed analytics becomes query first universal access plus workload-driven database schema and instance evolution.

Databases (Core).title: Taming Multi-Dimensional Skew in Sparse Matrix Multiplication with Contention-Aware Scheduling [Technical Report]
Databases (Core).summary:
Sparse general matrix-matrix multiplication (SpGEMM) is a key kernel in graph analytics, relational queries, and machine learning. Yet, its performance remains a significant challenge, due to the inherent sparsity and, more critically, the prevalent skew patterns often found in real-world workloads. This paper investigates this problem and demonstrates that an unbalanced workload distribution is the main culprit, harming performance through two co-existing root causes: first, multi-dimensional skew, where imbalance across computation cost, output density, and data locality cannot be captured by any single balancing metric; and second, cache contention, where dense substructures induce severe on-chip interference.
  To that end, we propose adaptive morsel scheduling (AMS), a dynamic scheduling framework that decouples skew dimensions via fixed-result-size morsels and integrates contention-aware load balancing (CALB) and data-conscious simultaneous multithreading activator (SMTact) to alleviate cache-level contention, alongside a hybrid accumulation mechanism (HYB) that adaptively selects the best accumulator per morsel. Evaluations across matrix squaring, relational queries, graph analytics, and other sparse matrix kernels show that AMS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on skewed workloads while maintaining comparable performance on non-skewed ones. These gains, along with improved bandwidth utilization, remain valid across a wide range of workloads and hardware systems.

Databases (Core).title: Synchronized Rebuilds:The Hidden Cost of Concurrent Inserts in Learned Indexes
Databases (Core).summary: Nine years after learned indexes were proposed, their advantage on read-mostly data is well established, and a standard benchmark rates their best concurrent version as almost ready for use. Across more than 4000 runs of 13 indexes, we find that each design pays for concurrent inserts in a different way. Gapped-array indexes rebuild their nodes in synchronized bursts, at positions that follow from three constants in the source. Model-placement indexes use three to four times the memory, buffered indexes take two to three times as long. Three of five concurrent learned indexes lost keys or stopped making progress. Standard benchmarks miss both the bursts and the lost keys. The bursts cost far more than in B-trees because each rebuild copies a node a thousand times larger than a page and, under concurrency, blocks every operation that reaches the node. The typical B-tree fix of randomizing node density only spreads the bursts out, while smaller nodes trade them for longer run times at scale. Two standard systems techniques remove them: a buffer that exists only while a node is rebuilt, and background rebuilds. We show that on 400M real keys, these techniques reduce the number of inserts whose latency exceeds 100$μ$s by two orders of magnitude at one thread, and by one at sixteen when spare cores run the background threads, at a third to half the run time of the buffered designs.

Databases (Core).title: CoPE-CGL: Community-aware Prototype Extraction for Replay-Free Continual Graph Learning
Databases (Core).summary: Continual graph learning (CGL) maintains models as graphs evolve without retraining from scratch, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Existing methods typically target either transductive or inductive settings and often store past subgraphs or require task identifiers at inference. We propose Community-aware Prototype Extraction for Continual Graph Learning (CoPE-CGL), a replay-free framework that uses a parameter-free structural prior, precomputed by multi-hop Laplacian smoothing, to anchor learning, memory, and inference. CoPE-CGL combines topology-infused bottleneck adaptation, community-level prototypes, and dynamic routing by majority vote over node-to-prototype matches. The default protocol assumes each test graph comes from one learned task; a node-level variant handles mixed-task graphs. Each task adds at most a constant amount of storage, with no past graph data retained. At equal storage and without task identifiers, CoPE-CGL matches the strongest replay baseline even when it receives true task identifiers: average performance (AP) is 95.17% and 95.72% versus 94.28% and 95.82% on Arxiv and CoraFull, respectively, with 5.9-14.0 times faster runtime and zero forgetting. Across four transductive and three inductive benchmarks and mixed streams, CoPE-CGL exceeds the second-best of up to eleven baselines by up to 1.41, 6.32, and 9.33 AP percentage points, respectively. It runs 1.3-7.9 times faster end-to-end than the most accurate competitor on each benchmark and scales to the largest benchmark graph. On graphs mixing two tasks, its node-level variant achieves the best AP among CGL methods. The design targets homophilic graphs with community structure.

Databases (Core).title: Revision-Bound Evidence Cuts: Authenticated Queries and Contextual Witness Capacity
Databases (Core).summary: Authentic records can support unauthorized narratives when their qualifications, query scope, or counterevidence are silently dropped. We present revision-bound evidence cuts, a framework for authenticating both supporting and opposing inference obligations across changing source versions. Signed complete-update frontiers permit transport of unaffected certificates, alternative-cut recovery, and an exact certified-reuse radius given by a frontier-hypergraph transversal number. Their source obligations induce an integral model of context-bound authorization. To secure database-derived claims, we introduce an authenticated relational query contract that binds original source records, complete selected bags, counting units, parameters, and aggregates independently of execution strategy. A full-source verifier checks 16,824 Chogha Mish records across SQLite scans, indexes, and materialized views; three valid strategies agree and eight contract/view mutations are rejected. A separate 340-row NISP cohort shows that changing the admitted weighting rule can reverse a comparison while preserving every source record. A frozen English text-to-frame compiler produces qualified evidence receipts, with linguistic accuracy evaluated separately from cryptographic integrity. We also separate logical-source from transport commitments so lossless re-encoding need not invalidate unchanged scientific evidence. The SCENE prototype evaluates signed revisions, authenticated queries, scoped disclosures, and adversarial mutations at scales reaching one million source records. These guarantees rely on declared policies and independently pinned trust roots; they authenticate specified computations and obligations, not historical truth, complete counterevidence, or institutional endorsement.

Databases (Core).title: What Does an Ontology Catch? Curated, LLM-Generated and Data-Derived Ontologies as Checkers of LLM Agents over Knowledge Graphs
Databases (Core).summary: LLM agents that answer questions over Web knowledge graphs are increasingly wrapped in checks derived from the graph's ontology, on the assumption that a formal schema makes a reliable judge. Yet a checker can be wrong as well: it can miss errors, and it can flag correct answers and push the agent into "fixing" them. Whether a curated ontology is worth its cost as such a judge, and how it compares with an ontology an LLM writes or a schema mined from the data, is unknown. We make the checker itself the object of study. Across curated, LLM-generated and data-derived ontologies, used as prompt context, as a checker, or both, and across open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph of nearly $10^{9}$ triples, we account for what ontology-derived checks catch and what they wrongly flag. We show how each source trades caught errors against false alarms, how a curated schema used as published can contradict its own data, which errors structural checks miss, and whether combining sources or giving the agent the checker's specific feedback pays off. On UniProt, the curated ontology flags more correct answers than either an ontology derived from the data or one an LLM derives from a summary of the data with masked identifiers. On real agent answers, its flags are only marginally more precise than random flags.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = Ψ(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $Ψ$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Corrupted but Correct: Why Vision-Language Models Lie to Themselves Internally
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: A targeted adversarial perturbation can drive a vision-language model's (VLM's) teacher-forced training loss for a fixed target caption to near zero, yet the same model, allowed to generate freely, produces the original, correct description with no trace of the target. We call this dissociation the train/inference gap, and give it a precise mechanistic account on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct using a controlled two-stage PGD attack on 200 held-out COCO images. First, we show that image-level pixel statistics, including a correctly re-implemented, texture-based attackability measure from the CNN robustness literature, have essentially no predictive power over which images are corrupted (best predictor r=-0.050, p=0.484; ridge regression R^2=0.069). Second, using the logit lens, we localise the gap to a single autoregressive step: the rank of the target token, conditioned on the correct first token already being generated, is fixed at exactly 3,488 out of 152,064 vocabulary entries for every image and every condition, with zero variance. Third, tracking target-token rank across all 28 LLM decoder layers reveals that the visual encoder corrupts every image's representation by a comparable margin regardless of eventual outcome, but the language model decoder then differentially arbitrates: amplifying the corrupted signal for susceptible images and actively suppressing it, past its clean-image baseline, for resistant ones (p<0.001, rank-biserial r=0.579). A linear probe on the merger hidden state separates these two outcomes with AUC=0.858, though we flag a circularity concern in this estimate. Together these results argue that adversarial robustness in autoregressive VLMs is substantially a property of the language decoder's prior, not the visual encoder, with direct implications for where faithfulness evaluations and defenses for deployed VLM systems should be targeted.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Agent-Conditioned Routing: Diverse Reasoning Paths Within One Frozen Model
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Generating several solutions can expose alternative methods, but additional trajectories often paraphrase one dominant approach. We investigate whether the conditional capacity of a frozen sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model can provide such diversity from one problem prompt, without user-assigned roles, prescribed methods, fine-tuning, or model copies. Agent-Conditioned Routing (ACR) assigns $m$ parallel trajectories persistent, untrained shared/private expert-eligibility masks while preserving the learned, input-dependent token router. On a screened 126-question multi-mode mathematics and physics benchmark, with model judges reading the reported derivations in full, we count the number of problems yielding at least two distinct primary methods among soft-correct solutions in four trajectories. ACR reaches approximately twice as many such problems as the strongest temperature setting under GLM 5.3 (37.3 versus 18.7), and 1.67 times as many under GPT-5.6 Sol (45.00 versus 27.00), at matched output budgets. A blinded four-expert audit on a stratified sample of 30 problems also finds more multi-method solutions with ACR on both backbones, with lower correctness. Matched-eligibility ablations show modest multi-method count advantages for ACR, while token-resampled masks attain higher correctness. An informed sequential prompt elicits more diversity still, using previous solutions and explicit requests for alternative methods. ACR adds about 160 KiB of mask state. In a three-problem microbenchmark capped at 1,024 tokens, its latency and peak VRAM usage remain within 3% of batched temperature sampling.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: SQuID: A Benchmark for Quantitative Spatial Reasoning on Satellite Imagery
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) describe satellite images fluently but struggle with the quantitative spatial reasoning that remote sensing (RS) analysts perform routinely, such as counting buildings, measuring forest area in hectares and computing distances in meters. We introduce SQuID (Satellite Quantitative Intelligence Dataset), a benchmark of 2,000 questions over 587 images from four sources at 0.3 to 1.0 m ground sampling distance, covering 24 question types in three difficulty tiers. Answers are computed from curated segmentation masks or, for 50 questions, from human consensus, and numeric answers are scored against tolerance ranges informed by human annotations. SQuID also releases the reference masks behind its answers, so that modular systems can be evaluated using reference rather than predicted masks, and 75,687 training question-answer pairs on disjoint images (SQuID-Train). Among 15 evaluated systems, the best zero-shot end-to-end VLM reaches 28.1%, and RS-specialized VLMs score lower. As a baseline, we propose QASR (Quantitative Agentic Spatial Reasoning), in which an LLM writes a program that segments the image and measures the masks with geometric operators. QASR reaches 42.0%. On the 1,950 mask-derived questions, running its programs on the reference masks instead of predicted masks raises accuracy from 42.2% to 82.6%, so segmentation is its main source of error. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B on SQuID-Train raises its accuracy from 16.1% to 40.7%, close to QASR. Multi-condition questions (Tier 3) remain the hardest in every setting, at 62.0% for QASR with reference masks and 13.2% after fine-tuning. These results leave clear room for end-to-end models that learn metric spatial reasoning, and SQuID provides the data to train and evaluate them.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: From Legacy Fortran to Portable Kokkos: An Autonomous Agentic AI Workflow
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Scientific applications continue to rely on legacy Fortran codebases originally developed for homogeneous, CPU-based systems. As High-Performance Computing (HPC) shifts toward heterogeneous GPU-accelerated architectures, many accelerators lack native Fortran bindings, creating an urgent need to modernize legacy codes for portability. Frameworks like Kokkos provide performance portability and a single-source C++ abstraction, but manual Fortran-to-Kokkos porting demands significant expertise and time. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in source-to-source code generation, yet their use in fully autonomous workflows for translating and optimizing parallel code remains largely unexplored, especially for performance portability across diverse hardware. This paper presents an agentic AI workflow where specialized LLM "agents" collaborate to translate, validate, compile, run, test, debug, and optimize Fortran kernels into portable Kokkos C++ programs. Results show the pipeline modernizes a range of benchmark kernels, producing performance-portable Kokkos codes across hardware partitions. Paid OpenAI models such as GPT-5 and o4-mini-high executed the workflow for only a few U.S. dollars, generating optimized codes that surpassed Fortran baselines, whereas open-source models like Llama4-Maverick often failed to yield functional codes. This work demonstrates the feasibility of agentic AI for Fortran-to-Kokkos transformation and offers a pathway for autonomously modernizing legacy scientific applications to run portably and efficiently on diverse supercomputers. It further highlights the potential of LLM-driven agentic systems to perform structured, domain-specific reasoning tasks in scientific and systems-oriented applications.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Optimal Experiments for Partial Causal Effect Identification
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Causal queries are often only partially identifiable from observational data, and experiments that could tighten the resulting bounds are typically costly. We study the problem of selecting, prior to observing experimental outcomes, a cost-constrained subset of experiments that maximally tightens bounds on a target query. We formalize this as the max-potency problem, where epistemic potency measures the worst-case reduction in bound width guaranteed by an experiment, and show that this problem is NP-hard via a reduction from 0-1 knapsack. Building on the polynomial-programming framework of Duarte et al. (2023), we give a general procedure for evaluating epistemic potency in discrete settings. To control the super-exponential search space, we introduce two graphical pruning criteria that depend only on the causal graph and the query: a novel path-interception rule that exploits district structure to certify zero potency in linear time, and an identifiability check based on the ID algorithm. On Erdos-Renyi random graphs and 11 bnlearn benchmark networks, the two criteria together prune 50-88% of candidate experiments on average without solving a single polynomial program. For the general subset search, we show that ID-pruned experiments are combinatorially inert, yielding a super-exponential reduction in the number of subsets evaluated. We close with an end-to-end demonstration on observational NHANES data, selecting optimal experiments for estimating the effect of physical activity on diabetes.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Flowette: Flow Matching with Graphette Priors for Graph Generation

Our model promotes topology-aware alignment through optimal transport-based coupling and preserves structural fidelity through endpoint- and chemistry-aware regularisation. To incorporate domain-driven structural priors, we introduce graphettes, a new probabilistic family of graph structure models that generalize graphons via controlled structural edits for motifs such as rings, stars, and trees. We theoretically analyze the coupling, invariance, and structural properties of the framework, evaluate it on synthetic and molecular benchmarks, and isolate the contributions of the structural prior, the optimal-transport coupling, and the regularisation terms through controlled ablations. Flowette achieves competitive performance overall, attaining state-of-the-art results on several metrics across multiple benchmarks, highlighting the effectiveness of combining structural priors with flow-based training for modeling complex graph distributions.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: Reliable probability estimates are critical in many machine learning applications, yet modern classifiers are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration provides a simple and widely used solution, but the large number of proposed methods, combined with small-scale and inconsistent evaluations, makes it difficult to determine which approaches are truly effective in practice. We introduce a large-scale, standardized benchmark for post-hoc calibration, covering nearly 2000 experiments across tabular and computer vision tasks, including binary, multiclass, and large-scale classification settings. Our benchmark aggregates predictions from a diverse set of classical models, modern deep learning architectures, and foundation models, and provides unified, reproducible implementations of dozens of calibration methods within a common evaluation framework. We argue that Post-Hoc Improvement (PHI) in proper scoring rules offers a principled alternative to traditional calibration error estimators for comparing post-hoc methods, capturing both calibration quality and potential degradation to the model's predictive performance. Using this framework, we conduct the most comprehensive empirical study of post-hoc calibration to date. Our results reveal consistent patterns across domains: smooth calibration functions outperform binning-based approaches, dedicated multiclass methods are essential in high-dimensional settings, and generic machine learning models are not competitive without calibration-specific design. To facilitate future research, we release all data, code, and evaluation tools, providing a plug-and-play benchmark for developing and comparing calibration methods.

Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.title: Learning Lotteries with Minimal Stakeholder Violations from Membership Queries
Artificial Intelligence (Top Venues & La.summary: An AI developer often has several candidate versions of a system and can deploy a mixture of them, sending each request to a randomly chosen version, as in A/B testing. Each stakeholder (e.g., a safety team, a regulator, or a customer with private test data) accepts a mixture exactly when its expected performance (e.g., its rate of harmful replies) meets the stakeholder's own standard, which the developer can learn only by asking whether a proposed mixture is acceptable. We model this as choosing a lottery over $m$ alternatives for $n$ agents, each of whom accepts exactly the lotteries in an unknown halfspace and answers such binary membership queries. While Choo et al. (ICML 2026) sought a lottery that every agent accepts, none may exist when, say, safety and helpfulness requirements conflict, so we minimize the number of rejecting agents. We show that this problem is APX-hard even when all halfspaces are known and all utilities are $0$ or $1$. We then give exact algorithms that run in polynomial time when $m$ is constant, and in quasi-polynomial time when, for a constant $η$, some optimal lottery has no accepting agent within $η$ of its threshold. When only some agents can be queried, optimizing over a uniform sample of agents gives additive and relative guarantees for the whole population, with a sample size that does not depend on $n$, and a linear program gives a polynomial-time method for any $m$. On the other hand, for $m\ge 3$, a deterministic algorithm that queries only $K$ distinct agents cannot guarantee fewer than $n-K$ extra rejections, and this is achievable; in other words, it can guarantee nothing for the agents it does not ask. Small synthetic experiments indicate that our worst-case bounds are conservative on random instances.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = Ψ(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $Ψ$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Scaling Reasoning Efficiently via Relaxed On-Policy Distillation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a promising approach for transferring reasoning capabilities to capacity-constrained models, yet sampled-token OPD often suffers from entropy collapse and negative transfer. We identify uniform credit allocation as a key bottleneck: existing objectives obtain dense teacher feedback on student-generated trajectories, but apply it uniformly across sampled tokens despite highly heterogeneous token-level signals. Most tokens carry redundant near-zero credit, while rare heavy-tailed negative credits can dominate updates and prematurely suppress plausible reasoning trajectories. We introduce REOPOLD (Relaxed On-Policy Distillation), a framework that relaxes this uniform assignment by controlling where teacher feedback is applied, how strongly it affects the update, and when the allocation rule changes during training. Across diverse reasoning tasks, REOPOLD improves sampled-token OPD over recent post-training baselines with up to 12x higher sample efficiency, and extends to cross-vocabulary distillation, self-distillation, and test-time scaling.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Adapting foundation models to a new task within or beyond the training domain is the de facto standard for building specialized machine learning models. Recently, Visual Prompting (VP) has emerged as a promising technique for efficient knowledge transfer. As new foundation model families~(like Mamba) get introduced and VP pipelines such as AutoVP reach greater maturity, we find a growing need for a systematic evaluation of current approaches. In this work, we assess the performance of the latest models, comparing them to earlier architectures and alternative fine-tuning methods, to better understand the progress, challenges and opportunities in the field of efficient fine-tuning under resource limitations. Towards this goal, this paper provides a concise empirical overview of the interactions among foundation model families (Attention-, Convolution-, and Mamba-based) and transfer paradigms: VP, Linear Probing (LP), Full Fine-tuning (FFT) and Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Our work builds up on previous findings by broadening the selection of evaluated models and techniques while tuning hyperparameters. In the interest of delivering practical guidelines for the user, we also explore application of prevalent regularization techniques to boost performance in the context of VP.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: STeP-TS: Shared Temporal Filters with Pruning for Time Series
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Multivariate time series forecasting requires capturing temporal dependencies across multiple scales while accounting for both shared and variable-specific dynamics. Compact forecasting models have emerged as an attractive alternative to increasingly large architectures, but preserving strong predictive performance within tight computational and memory budgets remains challenging. We propose a compact one-layer convolutional framework that learns a shared bank of multi-scale temporal filters of each variable. Lightweight variable-specific scalar weights determine the contribution of each temporal component, enabling the model to capture shared temporal structure while adapting to variable-specific dynamics. The learned weights and filter-output energy further provide a natural signal for structured pruning of convolutional filters, reducing computational complexity with minimal degradation in forecasting performance. We additionally introduce an amplitude-adaptive normalization mechanism that preserves variable-dependent temporal amplitudes. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate forecasting performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially fewer parameters and inference FLOPs and achieving low per-sample latency.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: An Input Skip Can Reparameterize a VAE Without Improving the Generator
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: An input skip can reduce reconstruction error while leaving a model's distribution of new samples unchanged. For a Gaussian variational autoencoder (VAE) with constant input skip $0\leqα<1$, a model without a skip can be written in skip form by multiplying its decoder output by $b=1-α$ and its noise variance by $b^2$. The distribution of observations and latent variables and its exact generative scores stay the same, while reconstruction mean squared error (MSE) is multiplied by $b^2$. Separate training can produce different generators because optimization depends on the parameter coordinates. In a Gaussian experiment with known density, changing skip and observation variance together reduces MSE but worsens energy score and the estimate of negative log density from importance sampling. On seven annual Deep-ocean Assessment and Reporting of Tsunamis (DART) records, energy score differences at the same observation variance have both signs on four original records and favor the skip on three records from 2018. Probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA) has lower mean energy scores than every neural DART fit. With the encoder and decoder kept the same, estimating observation variance from training reconstruction error can also worsen energy score. Assessing generation requires more than reconstruction error.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: LinMix: Data Mixing as Linear Domain Attribution
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Language model performance depends strongly on the mixture of domains in the pretraining data corpus. Popular data mixing methods select these domain weights by training many small proxy models on random mixes and then fitting a regression model to predict performance from the mix. We recognize this practice as a domain attribution problem, where the regression measures each domain's contribution to the target metric. Through this lens, the standard Dirichlet sampling of proxy data mixes is a poor regression design that requires tuning and cannot support a linear fit for hundreds of domains. Building on classical optimal experimental design, we introduce LinMix, which samples mixes at the vertices of the capped simplex so that each domain is at its cap or absent. This hyperparameter-free vertex sampling decorrelates domain effects, enabling an interpretable linear model whose coefficients are the domain attributions. The optimal mix given by LinMix provably keeps only domains with positive attribution values and requires no search over candidate mixes. We further establish the optimality of vertex sampling, and prove that Dirichlet sampling inflates the attribution error when its mixes concentrate around the prior data mix. Pretraining experiments with 1B-parameter OLMo2 and 4B Qwen3.5 language models show that LinMix outperforms Dirichlet-based data mixing across reasoning, code, and math benchmarks, with relative gains of 46% on MBPP and 14% on GSM8K. At 288 fine-grained domains, only vertex sampling supports a linear fit, and LinMix improves benchmark accuracy by 11% on average over the best nonlinear baseline.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Agent-Conditioned Routing: Diverse Reasoning Paths Within One Frozen Model
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Generating several solutions can expose alternative methods, but additional trajectories often paraphrase one dominant approach. We investigate whether the conditional capacity of a frozen sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model can provide such diversity from one problem prompt, without user-assigned roles, prescribed methods, fine-tuning, or model copies. Agent-Conditioned Routing (ACR) assigns $m$ parallel trajectories persistent, untrained shared/private expert-eligibility masks while preserving the learned, input-dependent token router. On a screened 126-question multi-mode mathematics and physics benchmark, with model judges reading the reported derivations in full, we count the number of problems yielding at least two distinct primary methods among soft-correct solutions in four trajectories. ACR reaches approximately twice as many such problems as the strongest temperature setting under GLM 5.3 (37.3 versus 18.7), and 1.67 times as many under GPT-5.6 Sol (45.00 versus 27.00), at matched output budgets. A blinded four-expert audit on a stratified sample of 30 problems also finds more multi-method solutions with ACR on both backbones, with lower correctness. Matched-eligibility ablations show modest multi-method count advantages for ACR, while token-resampled masks attain higher correctness. An informed sequential prompt elicits more diversity still, using previous solutions and explicit requests for alternative methods. ACR adds about 160 KiB of mask state. In a three-problem microbenchmark capped at 1,024 tokens, its latency and peak VRAM usage remain within 3% of batched temperature sampling.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: From Legacy Fortran to Portable Kokkos: An Autonomous Agentic AI Workflow
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Scientific applications continue to rely on legacy Fortran codebases originally developed for homogeneous, CPU-based systems. As High-Performance Computing (HPC) shifts toward heterogeneous GPU-accelerated architectures, many accelerators lack native Fortran bindings, creating an urgent need to modernize legacy codes for portability. Frameworks like Kokkos provide performance portability and a single-source C++ abstraction, but manual Fortran-to-Kokkos porting demands significant expertise and time. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in source-to-source code generation, yet their use in fully autonomous workflows for translating and optimizing parallel code remains largely unexplored, especially for performance portability across diverse hardware. This paper presents an agentic AI workflow where specialized LLM "agents" collaborate to translate, validate, compile, run, test, debug, and optimize Fortran kernels into portable Kokkos C++ programs. Results show the pipeline modernizes a range of benchmark kernels, producing performance-portable Kokkos codes across hardware partitions. Paid OpenAI models such as GPT-5 and o4-mini-high executed the workflow for only a few U.S. dollars, generating optimized codes that surpassed Fortran baselines, whereas open-source models like Llama4-Maverick often failed to yield functional codes. This work demonstrates the feasibility of agentic AI for Fortran-to-Kokkos transformation and offers a pathway for autonomously modernizing legacy scientific applications to run portably and efficiently on diverse supercomputers. It further highlights the potential of LLM-driven agentic systems to perform structured, domain-specific reasoning tasks in scientific and systems-oriented applications.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Nash Incentive-compatible Online Mechanism Learning via Weakly Differentially Private Online Learning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: We study a multi-round mechanism design problem, where we interact with a set of agents over a sequence of rounds. We wish to design an incentive-compatible (IC) online learning scheme to maximize an application-specific objective within a given class of mechanisms, without prior knowledge of the agents' type distributions. Even if each mechanism in this class is IC in a single round, if an algorithm naively chooses from this class on each round, the entire learning process may not be IC against non-myopic buyers who appear over multiple rounds. On each round, our method randomly chooses between the recommendation of a weakly differentially private online learning algorithm (e.g., Hedge), and a commitment mechanism which penalizes non-truthful behavior. Our method is IC and achieves $O(T^{\frac{1+h}{2}})$ regret for the application-specific objective in an adversarial setting, where $h$ quantifies the long-sightedness of the agents. When compared to prior work, our approach is conceptually simpler,it applies to general mechanism design problems (beyond auctions), and its regret scales gracefully with the size of the mechanism class.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: PGID: Progressive Guided Inversion and Denoising for Robust Watermark Detection
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: With the proliferation of AI-generated images, digital watermarking has become an essential safeguard for protecting intellectual property and mitigating malicious exploitation. Recent works on semantic watermarking have enabled efficient copyright protection for diffusion models. However, the dependence of semantic watermarking on diffusion inversion for watermark detection creates a critical vulnerability. Imprint removal and forgery attacks exploit this weakness to produce deceptive results. Our analysis reveals that these attacks succeed by displacing watermarked latents into the unwatermarked region, while guiding unwatermarked latents into the watermarked region. Based on that, we propose Progressive Guided Inversion and Denoising (PGID), the first plug-and-play, training-free noise extraction framework designed to defend against both attack strategies. PGID effectively defends by projecting perturbed latents back to the region where they originally belong. The projection is achieved by eliminating intermediate latent deflections and mitigating adversarial perturbations through progressive inversion-denoising cycles. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple schemes demonstrate that PGID successfully restores detection reliability by recovering removed watermarks and identifying forged instances.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Flowette: Flow Matching with Graphette Priors for Graph Generation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: We study generative modeling of graphs with recurring subgraph motifs. We propose Flowette, a continuous flow matching framework that employs a graph neural network-based transformer to learn a velocity field over graph representations with node and edge attributes. Our model promotes topology-aware alignment through optimal transport-based coupling and preserves structural fidelity through endpoint- and chemistry-aware regularisation. To incorporate domain-driven structural priors, we introduce graphettes, a new probabilistic family of graph structure models that generalize graphons via controlled structural edits for motifs such as rings, stars, and trees. We theoretically analyze the coupling, invariance, and structural properties of the framework, evaluate it on synthetic and molecular benchmarks, and isolate the contributions of the structural prior, the optimal-transport coupling, and the regularisation terms through controlled ablations. Flowette achieves competitive performance overall, attaining state-of-the-art results on several metrics across multiple benchmarks, highlighting the effectiveness of combining structural priors with flow-based training for modeling complex graph distributions.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Reliable probability estimates are critical in many machine learning applications, yet modern classifiers are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration provides a simple and widely used solution, but the large number of proposed methods, combined with small-scale and inconsistent evaluations, makes it difficult to determine which approaches are truly effective in practice. We introduce a large-scale, standardized benchmark for post-hoc calibration, covering nearly 2000 experiments across tabular and computer vision tasks, including binary, multiclass, and large-scale classification settings. Our benchmark aggregates predictions from a diverse set of classical models, modern deep learning architectures, and foundation models, and provides unified, reproducible implementations of dozens of calibration methods within a common evaluation framework. We argue that Post-Hoc Improvement (PHI) in proper scoring rules offers a principled alternative to traditional calibration error estimators for comparing post-hoc methods, capturing both calibration quality and potential degradation to the model's predictive performance. Using this framework, we conduct the most comprehensive empirical study of post-hoc calibration to date. Our results reveal consistent patterns across domains: smooth calibration functions outperform binning-based approaches, dedicated multiclass methods are essential in high-dimensional settings, and generic machine learning models are not competitive without calibration-specific design. To facilitate future research, we release all data, code, and evaluation tools, providing a plug-and-play benchmark for developing and comparing calibration methods.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: COMPOT: Calibration-Optimized Matrix Procrustes Orthogonalization for Transformers Compression
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Post-training compression of transformer models commonly relies on truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) strategies leading to low-rank approximations of the original model weights. However, the underlying single shared subspace modeling can degrade accuracy even at moderate compression. Sparse dictionary learning provides a more flexible union-of-subspaces representation, but existing approaches often suffer from costly iterative dictionary and coefficient updates. We propose $\textbf{COMPOT}$ ($\textbf{C}$alibration-$\textbf{O}$ptimized $\textbf{M}$atrix $\textbf{P}$rocrustes $\textbf{O}$rthogonalization for $\textbf{T}$ransformers), a training-free compression framework that uses a small calibration dataset to estimate a sparse weight factorization. COMPOT employs orthogonal dictionaries that enable closed-form Procrustes updates for the dictionary and analytical single-step sparse coding for the coefficients, reducing significantly the overall optimization cost. To handle heterogeneous layer sensitivity under a global compression budget, COMPOT further introduces a one-shot dynamic allocation strategy that adaptively redistributes layer-wise compression rates. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks show that COMPOT consistently delivers a superior quality-compression trade-off over strong low-rank and sparse baselines, while remaining fully compatible with post-training quantization for extreme compression.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Learning Pareto Stationary Fronts via Single-Pass Backpropagation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: We propose MOSEL (Multi-Objective Stackelberg Efficient Learning), a framework for a posteriori multi-objective optimization (MOO) in deep neural networks that recovers a full front of Pareto stationary solutions at the computational cost of standard single-objective training. MOSEL reformulates the problem as a bilevel optimization problem that leverages network modularity to decouple representation learning from objective-preference alignment. Casting the bilevel optimization problem as a Stackelberg game enables solving the original a posteriori MOO problem in a single forward-backward pass. As a result, MOSEL matches the time and memory efficiency of standard single-objective training while enabling scalable Pareto stationary front learning. Empirically, MOSEL uncovers diverse and optimal Pareto frontiers in strongly conflicting settings (e.g., fairness-accuracy). Remarkably, even in weakly conflicting regimes such as multi-task learning, it consistently converges to solutions closer to the utopia point, outperforming both standard single-objective training and specialized multi-task learning methods. These results highlight the broader potential of a posteriori MOO learning as a pathway to efficiently learn more diverse and robust representations, ultimately improving generalization.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Posterior-First Neural PDE Simulation: Inferring What Downstream Tasks Need from a Single Field
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Neural PDE simulators often receive only a single observed field at deployment. In this setting, a field-to-future predictor can collapse distinct latent problem states into the same deterministic interface, losing the ambiguity needed for reliable rollout and downstream decisions. We propose posterior-first neural PDE simulation, a task-to-target-to-interface paradigm: the declared downstream tasks determine the minimal task-sufficient problem state to infer, and the posterior over that state conditions the rollout and downstream queries. This posterior can be supplied by amortized posterior estimators, including simulation-based inference with learned summaries; our contribution is the target, the interface, and their theory. We show that Bayes downstream values factor through this posterior, proper scoring rules on refinement labels identify it as their population-risk minimizer, and deterministic collapse incurs an ambiguity barrier whenever the true posterior is non-Dirac. Synthetic exact-ambiguity experiments show that point-versus-posterior gaps track the predicted barrier. On metadata-hidden PDEBench tasks, posterior recovery reduces pooled rollout nRMSE from 0.175 to 0.132, closing 59.4% of the direct-to-oracle gap. Matched controls attribute the gains to task-aligned targeting and posterior deployment, and the gains persist with a latent-diffusion backbone. These results suggest that single-observation neural PDE simulation should be posterior-first rather than monolithic field-to-future prediction.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: V-LUMEN: Visual Lookup Memory for Embedding Scaling in Vision-Language Models
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Embedding-level scaling expands the capacity of language models through lookup-based memory rather than by increasing model depth, width, or dense computation. Extending this idea to vision-language models (VLMs) is challenging because visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, unlike discrete text tokens that naturally support n-gram lookup. We introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory for VLMs. V-LUMEN discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, builds spatially aware memory keys through spatial aggregation-based hashing, and modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals; all addressing is non-parametric, and the retrieved embeddings are fused into the backbone through a gated residual pathway. On five reasoning-intensive benchmarks, V-LUMEN substantially improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from the training data. At a matched parameter budget, moving part of a LoRA or MoE adapter's capacity into V-LUMEN preserves accuracy on two backbones, indicating that external visual memory is an independent capacity axis rather than a stronger adaptation method. Because lookup cost is constant in table size and incurred only once at prefill, this capacity grows in storage rather than in per-token compute. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/V-Lumen.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Does The Way You Plan Matter? An Empirical Study of Planning Representations for LLM Web Agents

Prior work suggests that many of these failures stem from weaknesses in planning, yet the impact of alternative natural language plan representations remains unexplored. To address this, we introduce PlanAhead, a static planner-executor framework that evaluates the impact of plan representation on agent performance. We first automatically categorize WebArena tasks into 3 difficulty levels, enabling consistent difficulty grading without human annotation. Then we systematically evaluate 4 different plan representations on the tasks categorized as hard: sequential subgoals, narrative, pseudocode, and checklist; across different families of multimodal LLM-powered agents(OpenAI, Alibaba, and Google). To account for stochastic variability, we introduce a novel decomposition of agent Success Rate (SR) into 2 interpretable evaluation metrics: Achievement Rate (AR) and Solved-Task Consistency (STC). Our results show that both, the plan formulation and the underlying LLM generating the plan, significantly influence web-agent robustness and task success.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Algorithmic Monoculture in Machine Learning-based Site-Specific Fertilizer Recommendation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Machine learning recommendations are often evaluated one model at a time, despite deployment across interconnected decision makers. A covariance-generalized formulation captures the dependence between model families. A two-model threshold characterizes when privately optimal monoculture is socially dominated, and a convex portfolio rule limits average private predictive regret. Nine model families across five Moroccan cereal systems provide a benchmark-based calibration. Under illustrative parameters and a 10% regret cap, accuracy-constrained diversification lowers modeled social loss in all five systems by 10.89-41.53% (mean 19.41%). Correlation sensitivity shows that highly dependent model errors attenuate the benefits of diversification. These counterfactual outcomes are not estimates of agronomic or monetary welfare; the framework identifies adoption architecture and error dependence as ecosystem-level evaluation variables.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. Existing TTA methods often obtain adaptation signals by updating model parameters or maintaining mutable memories, which can be costly and vulnerable to unknown samples. The head-induced basis decomposes each normalized feature into high-gain principal coordinates and low-gain tail coordinates. TALOR estimates a soft-routed affine correction in the principal subspace, combining a regime-level principal bias with a tail-conditioned slope that captures sample-level tail-to-principal coupling. Using weighted ridge regression, it subtracts this drift estimate from the principal coordinates, reconstructs the feature and feeds it into the source head. On the ImageNet-C benchmark with six csOOD datasets, TALOR outperforms the next-best UniEnt by 2.2% H-score while running 2.5x faster and using only 12% of its GPU memory; as a post-correction plug-in, it further boosts COME to 68.4% H-score with only 2% additional memory overhead.

To address model misspecification, we propose a doubly robust preference optimization algorithm that remains consistent when either the preference model or the reference policy is correctly specified (without requiring both). Our proposal demonstrates superior and more robust performance than state-of-the-art algorithms, both in theory and in practice. The code is available at https://github.com/DRPO4LLM/DRPO4LLM

In our sweep on two tasks, most batched runs finished in half the wall-clock time or less, and the fastest in about a quarter to a third. A simple runtime model explains the measured speedups under a finite worker pool, and batched settings also spend their metric-call and dollar budgets more efficiently. We frame the axes along which a reflective optimization step can scale in parallel, a first look at allocating a fixed optimization budget across them.
