Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Robust Flow Matching under Target Corruption and Label Noise
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Flow Matching (FM) is a strong framework for generative modeling due to its stable training and efficient sampling. However, FM assumes clean target data and labels, an assumption often violated in practice. We formulate FM training as a time-dependent regression problem over conditional vector fields and analyze how the two corruption types affect the objective: i) target corruption adds a time-dependent residual term that grows with time, ii) label noise causes updates to the wrong class-conditional vector field. Based on this analysis, we propose to improve FM robustness by mapping corruption-specific residual scores to sample weights. For target corruption, we propose the Temporal Residual Score (TRS), which emphasizes residual magnitudes at intermediate-to-late FM times, where clean and corrupted samples are more separable. For label noise, we propose the Comparative Conditional Score (CCS), which compares the residual of the observed class-conditional vector field against alternative class-conditional vector fields for the same trajectory and velocity target. Experiments across controlled corruption settings and real-world noisy labels show that the proposed methods improve robustness over standard FM and robust-training baselines, supporting corruption-specific residual structure as a practical basis for robust FM.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Self-Modeling Interventions can Modulate Emergent Misalignment
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Emergent misalignment (EM) has been linked to the activation of misaligned persona vectors and evil character traits, suggesting that EM operates through disruption of the model's aligned character rather than direct learning of harmful content. Motivated by this connection, we study self-modeling interventions: specifically self-recognition and self-reports as character-targeted interventions that are distinct from existing in-training defenses. We conduct two-stage finetuning experiments across three models (GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct) and multiple EM datasets to compare self-recognition finetuning against benign finetuning baselines (correct domain-specific data, general knowledge, and word counting), finding it an effective defense in both reversal and prevention settings. For prevention, only self-recognition finetuning consistently reduces misalignment without exacerbating any individual metric, suggesting that character fortification specifically drives prevention. We also conduct in-training experiments across these models to compare the effectiveness of self-reports with benign interleaving and inoculation prompting. We provide further evidence for EM's relation to the LLM's default character by showing that EM finetuning leads to fragmentation of LLM's identity self-reports, reduces self-recognition performance to about chance, artificially corrupting self-recognition exacerbates misalignment caused by EM finetuning, and finetuning on self-reports from EM finetuned models can transfer misalignment. Together, these findings reframe EM not as the adoption of a coherent misaligned persona but as the destabilization of aligned character.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: An Analytical Model of Compute-limited Multistage Training Pipelines
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Modern foundation models are trained through multiple stages, yet how these stages interact and how compute should be allocated across them remain poorly understood. We introduce an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining unsupervised pretraining with a linear autoencoder, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with noisy stepwise labels, and reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory and an operator-projection closure, we derive approximate low-dimensional learning dynamics that closely match simulations. We show that finite pretraining data imposes a representation-dependent performance limit, with Bayes classification error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio, and observe the same exponent in asymptotic SFT and RL errors. Better pretraining also reduces sensitivity to noisy supervision. SFT initialization shortens the initial RL plateau induced by sparse rewards, an effect we also observe in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Optimizing compute across all three stages reveals that the optimal allocation depends on supervision quality and total budget, with a non-monotonic dependence of the RL compute share on budget. Finally, a complementary compositional model shows how RL selectively strengthens task-relevant pretrained skills while largely preserving unused skills. Together, these results identify mechanisms linking representation quality, feedback structure, and compute allocation in multistage training.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Off-policy Learning with Excursion Policies
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) tries to learn the value of a target policy while data comes from a different behavior policy. This often requires trading off bias for variance or stability. One way to trade these off is to linearly interpolate between the behavior and target policies, but this represents only one point in a broader space of interpolation mechanisms. We introduce excursion policies--a structured alternative where the agent follows the target policy for a multi-step "excursion" before reverting to the behavior policy. We derive dynamic programming results for these policies, establishing the theoretical basis for their use in RL. We further develop provably sound off-policy temporal-difference (TD) algorithms for excursion value estimation. We find that excursion policies provide an efficiency-stability trade-off comparable to mixture policies in continuous control benchmarks, and our analysis illustrates conceptual differences in their behavior.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: CRAFT: Conflict-Resolved Aggregation for Federated Training
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: The aggregation of conflicting client updates remains a fundamental bottleneck in federated learning (FL) under heterogeneous data distributions. Naive averaging can produce a global update that improves the global objective while conflicting with specific clients, causing degradation for those clients. In this work, we propose CRAFT (Conflict-Resolved Aggregation for Federated Training), a new aggregation framework that treats the global update as a geometric correction problem. We formulate aggregation as finding the update closest to a reference direction while satisfying conflict-free alignment constraints. We derive a closed-form expression for the constrained optimization problem, avoiding the computational overhead of iterative solvers. Furthermore, we use a layer-wise adaptation to address conflicts at varying feature granularities. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that CRAFT promotes a common-descent structure and mitigates conflicts through its projection geometry. Extensive experiments on heterogeneous benchmarks demonstrate that CRAFT improves the accuracy of the global model while reducing performance disparity across clients compared with state-of-the-art baselines. The source code for CRAFT is available at https://github.com/tum-pbs/CRAFT.
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026. Funded by the European Union (Horizon Europe MSCA project ModConFlex, grant number 101073558)

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Deep Double Q-learning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Double Q-learning is a classical control algorithm that mitigates the maximization bias of Q-learning. To do so, it explicitly trains two independent action-value functions and uses them to decouple action-selection from action-evaluation when computing bootstrap targets. Double DQN adapts this decoupling to deep reinforcement learning (RL) but directly trains only a single action-value function and does not fully decouple its estimators. Consequently, the two estimators remain correlated, and overestimation persists. In this paper, we introduce Deep Double Q-learning (DDQL), a deep RL algorithm that explicitly trains two Q-functions through the Double Q-learning objective. DDQL stabilizes training through a combination of techniques, including lower replay ratios, longer target network update intervals, and shared layers. Across 57 Atari 2600 games, DDQL improves aggregate performance over Double DQN, outperforming it on 47 games while further reducing overestimation. We study key design choices of DDQL, including its network architecture, replay ratio, and minibatch sampling strategies.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Derivative-Informed Training of Neural Operators On-the-Fly via Sketched Tangent Consistency
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Derivative-informed training improves neural operators by directly supervising their input-output sensitivities, which is crucial when neural operators are used as differentiable surrogates for inverse problems, PDE-constrained optimization, design, and control. However, existing methods rely on offline-generated derivative labels, making data generation slow, storage-intensive, and difficult to adapt across datasets, resolutions, or perturbation bases. We propose sketched tangent consistency loss (sTCL), an on-the-fly derivative-informed training objective that, for PDEs with a known and differentiable residual, enforces sensitivity consistency directly from the governing equation without offline tangent labels or neural-operator architecture changes. sTCL uses randomly sketched input perturbations to provide a lightweight derivative-level physics constraint during training. However, raw forward-sensitivity residual penalties can fail for stiff, ill-conditioned, indefinite, or coupled saddle-point tangent operators. To address this, we introduce lightweight operator-aware loss-conditioning mechanisms selected by a simple tangent-operator decision rule. Across Helmholtz, nonlinear diffusion-reaction, Burgers, Allen-Cahn, and Navier-Stokes, with the same neural-operator backbone for all methods, the PDE-specific sTCL losses achieve solution and Jacobian accuracy comparable to offline derivative-informed training (DIFNO) while eliminating the offline derivative-data generation and storage pipeline. These results show that on-the-fly derivative-informed training need not merely amortize offline tangent-solve cost into training; with appropriate sketching and loss design, sTCL provides an effective drop-in path to derivative-informed neural operators. Code is available at https://github.com/Mou-group-UMN/Derivative-informed-training-on-the-fly.
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 24 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: LookThere! Sparse Vision by Reinforced Selection
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Vision transformers typically treat every image token as equally important, yet for most tasks in computer vision only a fraction are needed. Adaptive computation methods accelerate inference by choosing which tokens to process, but existing methods struggle at extreme sparsity and require heuristics that may not generalize like token diversity and attention scores. We address these limitations with LookThere, achieving a new pareto frontier in performance-compute trade-offs through an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that jointly trains a shallow input selector and a deep representation extractor. The selector learns where to look and the extractor learns what to see, together saving computation by selecting only what is worth processing for a given task without relying on auxiliary signals. We show that LookThere only selects the task-specific input, excelling at sparse recognition in high-resolution settings (traffic signs, billiards), and maintaining accuracy with as little as 0.2% of the input. It generalizes across tasks and models, including global recognition (ImageNet classification), local recognition (ADE20K segmentation), zero-shot classification (by distillation), and regression (counting). Across all settings, LookThere surpasses state-of-the-art selection to provide a general and scalable framework for specialized and efficient adaptive computation.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Wrong the Same Way: Cross-Prompt Sharing Both Suppresses and Amplifies Reward Hacking in RLVR
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Two accounts of how reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) interacts with an imperfect verifier coexist: in one, reward hacking is inherited from the base model; in the other, RL amplifies it. We study both in a controlled environment small enough to compute the entire response distribution exactly. We vary the universality of a leak, or the fraction of prompts that accept the same wrong response, and the verifier's static false-positive rate. At its KL-regularized optimum, RLVR acts as a filter that reweights the accepted set without altering its composition, so the hack rate is inherited exactly. Taking that as a null model, a known decomposition writes the drift from it as a sum over prompts of covariances between reward and the empirical tangent kernel. The terms from other prompts vanish without parameter sharing. With sharing, every prompt that accepts a wrong answer pushes it up and every prompt that rejects it pushes it down through the baseline, in proportion to the model's probability of producing it there. A shared-parameter policy thus drives a leak that few prompts accept below the base rate and amplifies one that most prompts accept. At every convergent learning rate under Adam, SGD, and sampled GRPO, hacking ends higher at high universality than at low, but whether either end crosses the base rate depends on the step size. Independent per-prompt copies remove the dependence. The direction of this push depends on neither the verifier's error rate nor universality alone, but on how much of the model's kernel-weighted probability of a wrong answer falls on prompts that accept it, which frozen base model controls support. Verifier fixes should target the mistakes the model repeats across prompts: two patches that remove equally many errors differ by up to 38 points of true accuracy. We propose this alignment as a hypothesis for why earlier studies disagree.
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).comment: Accepted at the Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training Workshop at NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Before Words, Beyond Speech: Evaluating Nonverbal Social Reasoning in Early Childhood
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Children's earliest years are a period of intense social learning, during which meaning is built through gaze, gesture, and physical contact. Yet, this critical aspect of social interaction remains under-evaluated in multimodal video understanding, as existing benchmarks prioritize the conversation-driven interactions of adults. We address this gap with \bench ($\textbf{N}$aturalistic $\textbf{E}$arly-childhood $\textbf{S}$ocial in$\textbf{T}$eractions), the first child-centric benchmark for nonverbal social reasoning. \bench comprises \totalvids manually annotated clips ($\sim$12s) curated for diversity across naturalistic settings, cultural contexts, and developmental stages. Beyond a lack of data, targeted model improvement in this domain is hindered by coarse evaluation schemas that conflate basic perception with higher-order reasoning. To resolve this, \bench introduces a compositional schema that builds atomic interaction cues into progressive levels of social reasoning: contextual, behavioral, interpersonal, and open-ended descriptions. Extensive analysis of state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reveals a stark performance collapse: despite strong contextual recognition, models exhibit substantial gaps in decoding precise behavioral and interpersonal cues. We trace these failures to specific biases, including poor consequence grounding and temporal sensitivity. Finally, we ground \bench in real-world applications by evaluating VLMs using domain adaptation strategies. Ultimately, \bench provides a rigorous testbed for advancing socially grounded artificial intelligence in early childhood. Project page: https://laubravo.github.io/nest_website/.
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).comment: Accepted as NeurIPS 2026 Spotlight paper. Project page at \hyperlink{https://laubravo.github.io/nest_website/}{this URL}

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Structured Kernel Surrogate Models for Multimodal Attribution
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: We study the problem of cross-sample modality attribution, which involves measuring how one modality in one sample affects the learning outcome in other multimodal samples. This problem is crucial in a multimodal system because a data modality (such as a text description) may be redundant for one sample (a self-explanatory image), but the same data modality would otherwise be uniquely informative for another sample, or informative when combined with other modalities. Prior work focuses on influence estimation at the level of one sample, and it remains an open question how one should capture the interactions across both samples and modalities. To capture scenarios like the above, we propose structured kernel surrogate models, which are surrogate mappings from both samples and modalities to the prediction outcome when they are trained together. We design an algorithm, SKS, which applies kernel ridge regression with a structured, compositional kernel on the selection states of individual samples and modalities. Specifically, the kernel function multiplies kernel-based similarity scores between every pair of data modalities for one sample and a pair of two samples. Additionally, we design a gradient-based estimation algorithm to efficiently estimate the structured kernel surrogate model. We evaluate our approach on two multimodal benchmarks, spanning a range of data modalities including satellite images, road networks, text, audio, and tabular data. We find that SKS achieves $57.8$% higher correlation with the true prediction outcomes than existing methods. In downstream data selection, SKS improves the average accuracy by $1.93$% over baselines. Models with data selected by SKS have lower Hessian traces, indicating a flatter loss surface. Using SKS to select satellite images identifies road segments, where accident scenes commonly occur, as opposed to background images.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: AGiR: Mitigating Gift Over-Reliance in Mixed-Motive Games
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: In this paper, we consider mixed-motive games (MMGs) which model various real-world multi-agent scenarios where self-interested agents must both cooperate and compete. We identify an issue with existing gifting methods, where agents become overly dependent on incoming gifts and fail to learn reward-yielding behaviors, a phenomenon we call gift over-reliance. To address this, we propose a refusal-augmented gifting framework that balances cooperation and competition in MMGs. Our approach introduces an adaptive refusal mechanism that allows agents to selectively reject a portion of received gifts from their policy-update signals, thereby mitigating gift over-reliance and preventing the agents from being exploited by other agents. This mechanism is gifting-method-agnostic, serving as a plug-in for existing schemes while enabling decentralized learning. We demonstrate that across diverse MMG environments and gifting schemes, our mechanism consistently reduces gift over-reliance and prevents lock-in to sacrificing policies, improving $α$-fairness as a result, without necessitating major changes to existing training pipelines.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: High Probability Risk Control for Online Policy Learning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: We study risk control for online policy learning, where an agent adaptively collects data and aims to learn a new policy whose risk stays below a tolerance threshold at every round with high probability. Such policy updates and data collection induce feedback covariate shift (FCS): observed data depend on history through evolving policies and the data-collection process. FCS brings two substantive problems for risk control: 1) efficient risk evaluation for each candidate policy and 2) valid policy selection with high-probability risk control. To address these, we propose a permutation-based weighted risk evaluator with weights efficiently approximated by the Sinkhorn algorithm and select policies whose estimated risk upper confidence bounds (UCB) fall below the target threshold, with the UCB obtained through a proposed Gaussian bootstrap method. Theoretically, we prove that our risk evaluator has a no-larger variance upper bound than that of the standard importance-weighted evaluator. Our policy control method also yields an asymptotically valid simultaneous risk bound and provides asymptotic high-probability risk control for the selected policy. Empirically, we evaluate our method on the online contextual bandit problem, safe question answering benchmark, and Medical Claim Filtering tasks. Our method maintains the target risk level, achieves lower risk than baseline methods, has lower variance in risk estimation, and achieves reliable policy selection with high-probability risk control. Further ablation studies support our theoretical claims.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: VIGOR: Benchmarking Visual Rationale Correctness in Multimodal Large Language Models
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are typically evaluated by whether they produce correct answers, but correctness alone does not reveal whether their outputs are supported by the right visual evidence. We introduce VIGOR, a benchmark for evaluating VIsually GrOunded Rationales in MLLMs. VIGOR represents visual rationales as explicit concepts paired with pixel-level groundings, covering multiple abstraction levels including low-level visual properties, intermediate structures, objects, parts and high-level motion, relations. To construct VIGOR at scale, we develop an automatic annotation framework that reuses existing dense supervision when available and generates missing concept groundings through proposal-based annotation followed by conservative multimodal verification. Using VIGOR, we evaluate whether MLLMs "look at what they say" by comparing model-derived visual evidence for each expressed concept against annotated ground-truth rationales. Our results show that current MLLMs exhibit limited visual rationale correctness and reveal distinct grounding failures across concept levels. VIGOR provides a benchmark and scalable data construction pipeline for studying whether MLLM outputs are supported by appropriate visual evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/deep-real/VIGOR

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: One Temperature to Rule Them All?
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Inference-time sampling is a central mechanism for improving large language models, with temperature controlling the tradeoff between reliability and diversity. While recent work suggests that varying temperature across samples can improve multi-sample inference, simple fixed-temperature schemes remain the standard in practice. We investigate this discrepancy in the canonical pass@K setting, asking when temperature diversity is useful, and when a single tuned temperature suffices. To this end, we analyze per-question success probabilities across multiple models and datasets, tracking how they vary with sampling temperature. We identify several consistent properties of these profiles, including that harder questions are less likely to share efficient sampling temperatures, although this trend is only logarithmic in hardness. We then derive an efficient method for evaluating the theoretically optimal multi-temperature allocation scheme, and show that although such a scheme improves performance, its gains over single-temperature baselines are typically modest when temperature is tuned as a function of the sampling budget K. We explain this phenomenon through mathematical mechanisms that we call dulling effects, and show how they ensure the robustness of temperature choices across different question distributions. Our results clarify when multi-temperature sampling is useful, and how temperatures should ideally be chosen.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: The Sampling Complexity of Condorcet Winner Identification in Dueling Bandits
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: We study best-arm identification in large-scale stochastic dueling bandits under the sole assumption that a Condorcet winner exists, i.e., an arm that wins each noisy pairwise comparison with probability at least $1/2$. We introduce a new identification procedure that exploits the full gap matrix $Δ_{i,j}=q_{i,j}-\tfrac12$ (where $q_{i,j}$ is the probability that arm $i$ beats arm $j$), rather than only the gaps between the Condorcet winner and the other arms. We derive high-probability, instance-dependent sample-complexity guarantees that (up to logarithmic factors) improve the best known ones by leveraging informative comparisons beyond those involving the winner. We complement these results with matching lower bounds that establish the optimality of our procedures in all regimes. Overall, our results reveal the general form of the sampling complexity, characterized by a trade-off between the cost of locating informative entries and the verification cost required to achieve the desired confidence. In particular, this complexity drastically differs from what is suggested by pure asymptotic results or by procedures that are tailored to Strongly Stochastic Transitive models.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Beyond the First Hit: Towards Tight Guarantees for $k$-means++
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove $R_k\le\frac{1163}{233}+2.108\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge3$ by a computer-assisted argument, and $R_k\le5+2.3139\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge2$ by a short analytic argument; here $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number. Since $H_{k-2}\le1+\ln k$, this lowers the leading coefficient of $\ln k$ from $5$ to $2.108$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$ exactly; both are suprema that are approached but not attained. On the lower side we prove $R_k\ge2(1+H_{k-1})$ for every $k$, and give a second family of lower bounds that is larger than this for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We instead track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit: a cluster left with a large residual cost is likely to be sampled again before it accumulates much of the logarithmic charge, and each repeat repairs it.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: PORT: Preference Optimization via Robust Token-Level Reweighting
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Preference optimization has become a central approach for aligning large language models with human values, but its effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of preference annotations. In practice, preference data is often noisy due to annotation errors and ambiguity. Existing robust preference optimization methods primarily operate at the sequence level, implicitly treating entire responses as uniformly correct or incorrect. However, rejected responses may still contain informative reasoning steps, while preferred responses can include subtle errors. In this work, we propose \textbf{P}reference \textbf{O}ptimization via \textbf{R}obust \textbf{T}oken-level reweighting \textbf{(PORT)}, a fine-grained framework for robust alignment under noisy preferences. PORT performs token-level reweighting using the empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) of token log-probabilities, yielding an efficient forward-pass-only proxy to gradient-norm penalization that selectively suppresses corrupted tokens without additional backward-pass computation. We provide theoretical analysis showing that PORT reduces the gradient bias from noisy preference labels by minimizing an upper bound on the bias term. Extensive experiments across diverse noise settings demonstrate that PORT consistently improves robustness and outperforms existing sequence-level baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/osu-srml/PORT
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, neurips 2026

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. \textsc{NarrativeBench} provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.comment: NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Dataset Track

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: HEARSAYBENCH: Can AI Navigate from Abstract Human Rights to Lived Lives?
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary:
As large language models (LLMs) reach users worldwide, personal counseling has emerged as one of their most consequential applications, sometimes in life-critical situations. Yet broader access does not mean equal support. The text these models learn from disproportionately reflects people with the freedom to act, embedding an implicit assumption that users can leave, report, seek help, or appeal. Existing benchmarks largely inherit this assumption, overlooking users whose agency is constrained by structural conditions such as war, statelessness, and displacement. Meanwhile, models are increasingly shaped by normative frameworks such as Constitutional AI, often grounded in ideals like human rights, even as many users live where those rights offer little protection or recourse.
  We introduce HEARSAYBENCH, a human-authored dataset of 400 test cases with in-region human verification grounded in scenarios where structural barriers stand between a person and the exercise of their rights. Built from United Nations and other human rights reports, the scenarios span over 80 regions and cover social, environmental, and personal constraints. Drawing on Nobel laureate Amartya Sen's Capabilities Approach, HEARSAYBENCH tests whether models can distinguish what a person is formally entitled to do from what they are actually able to do. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, every model infers a user's situation more accurately than it advises on it. Stronger models narrow this gap, but their recommendations remain unsafe to follow. Models may understand lives shaped by constraint, yet that knowledge remains hearsay if it cannot translate into advice people can act on. Those people are not alignment's long tail; they are among the users for whom good guidance matters most. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: A local language model layered with rule-based and neural detectors for clinical text de-identification: an open-source toolkit and evaluation
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary:
Objectives: To measure whether a locally hosted large language model (LLM), stacked with deterministic and clinical named-entity recognition (NER) detectors, finds more protected health information (PHI) than open tools, and at what precision.
  Materials and Methods: DeidSharp, an open-source .NET toolkit, combines the findings of pluggable detectors (patterns, a clinical NER model, a local 26B mixture-of-experts LLM) and fails closed on any detector error. Configurations fixed on tuning halves were compared, under a prespecified protocol, with deid, Philter, the Stanford/Penn de-identifier, OpenAI Privacy Filter and GLiNER on reporting halves of PhysioNet's nursing notes (889 spans) and semi-synthetic MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries (29,023 spans), and on synthetic ASQ-PHI queries, with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals.

In the discharge summaries, both stacks led Stanford/Penn by more than 20 points (recall-first 95.3%, +21.5, 20.5 to 22.4), almost entirely on generated untyped names; on typed labels all three exceeded 99%. All four prespecified comparisons held. No configuration beat deid significantly on its home corpus; Philter found more discharge-summary spans than the recall-first stack at 23 points lower precision.
  Discussion: The LLM was the main detector and NER added place names; asked to verify its own findings, the LLM discarded a quarter of true PHI.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: BFS-PO: Best-First Search for Large Reasoning Models
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have shown excellent performance in reasoning tasks using long Chains of Thought (CoTs). However, this has also led to a significant increase of computational costs and the generation of verbose output, a phenomenon known as overthinking. The tendency to overthink is often exacerbated by Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms such as GRPO/DAPO. In this paper, we propose BFS-PO, an RL algorithm which alleviates this problem using a Best-First Search exploration strategy. Specifically, the reasoning chains generated at training time by BFS-PO are organized into a search tree, within which the shortest correct sequence is selected as the best and expanded using a backtracking mechanism based on maximum entropy nodes. In this way, we bias the exploration of the solution space towards the search for increasingly shorter solutions, training the LRM to generate progressively more concise answers. Using different benchmarks and base LRMs, we show that BFS-PO can simultaneously increase the LRM accuracy and shorten its reasoning chains.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: SlotGuard: Stop Oversharing Private Local Context in LLM Agent Transcripts
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: LLM agents can expose private local context (e.g., paths, emails) and credentials (e.g., API keys) as agent observations (e.g., tool outputs, shell logs, and file reads) are appended to provider-bound transcripts. Existing placeholder redaction is brittle: it can miss embedded or cross-turn references, over-redact benign lookalikes, and destroy the structure useful for reasoning. SlotGuard rewrites structural bindings as typed, suffix-aware slots, replaces secrets with format-preserving synthetic values, links cross-turn references with a lightweight session graph, and restores raw values only inside the trusted runtime. On controlled repository-oriented agent transcripts, SlotGuard removes all 20,814 annotated structurally sensitive characters across 9,229 paths and reduces credential leakage to 0.0% across 852 planted values. It remains close to raw-transcript task success across four upstream models, while generic redaction drops to 2.5%. Deterministic transcript rewriting takes a median of 14.424 microseconds per agent turn, excluding the optional semantic detector. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: AI is used in much of the clinical trial pipeline. However, selecting the statistical design of a trial, a crucial step that determines how drug doses are tested on humans and evaluated, has seen almost no AI progress. LLMs appear to be a natural fit given their strengths in biomedical knowledge and statistical reasoning. Nevertheless, there is currently no appropriate way to evaluate such abilities because recent regulatory and methodological shifts, most notably FDA's Project Optimus, have redefined what constitutes a reasonable design and rendered many previous designs obsolete. To lay the groundwork for AI-assisted trial design, we introduce TrialDesignBench, a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design that is consistent with the latest FDA regulatory initiatives. This reference standard is produced through a formalization of the expert design process. We evaluate five frontier LLMs, none of which matches the reference standard. Our ablation experiments trace this performance gap to two main causes, inference of latent, unrecorded design determinants from trial sources (supplying them raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22) and structured decision-tree reasoning (+0.24). TrialDesignBench offers a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Correctness vs Efficiency: Behavior Control with Weight-Space Extrapolation in Code RL
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: A model trained with an imperfect reward in RL may learn to exploit the reward with undesired behavior. We study a controlled form of this problem in competitive programming. A program may pass small tests while violating the intended efficiency requirement on larger inputs. We construct a family of rewards that progressively relax the efficiency constraint, making the reward increasingly easy to exploit, and train separate policies. This sweep reveals a correctness-efficiency frontier. Relaxing the reward leads to less efficient programs and more resource-limit failures. Stricter rewards suppress these failures but increase correctness failures near the model's capability boundary. This frontier is also reflected in weight space. Interpolating between the resulting models reproduces the same behavioral change. More surprisingly, extrapolation in both directions further amplifies or suppresses it beyond the trained checkpoints. Extensive experiments show that this pattern holds across pure reasoning, tool use, and agentic coding, and at both 32B and 7B scales. This suggests a simple intervention for this form of reward hacking: use a loose reward to amplify the undesired behavior, use the weight-space difference to a strict-reward model as its steering vector, and then extrapolate past the strict model to suppress it.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: A core obstacle to alignment evaluation is evaluation awareness: capable models can tell when they are being tested rather than deployed, weakening the conclusions a safety evaluation can support. We present two techniques that make simulated alignment evaluations harder to distinguish from real deployments. Our first technique, critique refinement, spends additional inference-time compute on each simulator action: the simulator generates multiple candidate actions, refines them using feedback from an instance of the target model on how to make them more realistic, and continues the evaluation with the most deployment-like candidate. Our second technique, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target in an agent harness, reducing the gap between simulated and real deployment environments in coding settings. We test the techniques on multiple target models and find that applying both yields larger realism gains than either alone. We show that automated approaches can improve the realism of alignment evaluations, and that they compare favorably to spending the extra compute on more audit attempts.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Scientific research has long been driven by substantial human effort, from reviewing prior work and identifying research gaps to designing specific solutions. Recent advances in harness-based agent systems have given rise to increasingly capable Auto Researchers, which can autonomously carry out these tasks and, increasingly, entire end-to-end research workflows. Yet despite their rapidly growing capabilities, how closely the research decisions and outputs produced by auto researchers align with those of human experts remains underexplored. We investigate this gap through the lens of research reconstruction and study: Given comparable research context, how similar are the research decisions and outputs produced by Auto Researchers to those of human researchers in AI research? To answer this question, we introduce AutoResearcher-Human Research Similarity (AutoHRS), a stage-wise evaluation framework for assessing how faithfully auto researchers reconstruct human research artifacts across different stages of the scientific workflow. Using 152 ICLR oral papers as our corpus, we generate 456 research trajectories spanning different stages of the research process. Applying AutoHRS to these trajectories, we find that current Auto Researchers frequently fail to recover key research decisions and their resulting artifacts across multiple stages of the research process.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: LoopWeaver: Weaving Feedback Loops into Hierarchical Generation under Constraints
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Large Language Models face a multi-objective optimization problem in constrained long-text generation, balancing global structure, local coherence, and constraint satisfaction. We propose LoopWeaver, a hierarchical workflow with two sequential offline preference-optimization stages. Constraint-aware planning produces structured plans, feasibility filtering removes invalid plans, and a shared deterministic reward constructs preference pairs for plan-level and generation-level DPO. At inference time, LoopWeaver remains feed-forward: it generates and revises a complete plan, filters the revised plan, and then generates segments conditioned on the current sub-plan and running narrative. Results show improvements in both constraint accuracy and text quality across all four open-source backbones. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/cgtaa-cmyk/LoopWeaver.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Geometric Latent Reasoning Induces Shorter Generations in LLMs
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Large language models solve complex problems by generating lengthy chains of explicit reasoning tokens. While effective, this makes reasoning expensive, length-sensitive, and constrained to (discrete) natural language. While latent reasoning offers a continuous alternative, determining useful structures for intermediate latent states is an open challenge. In this paper, we formulate latent reasoning as a geometric path-approximation problem within the model's pretrained token-embedding space. We introduce Geometric Latent Reasoning (GLR), which uses a lightweight transition head to predict iterative direction updates in embedding space. Using textual chain-of-thought traces as anchors, GLR learns to approximate discrete reasoning trajectories while permitting continuous deviations from exact token embeddings. Evaluations on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using Qwen3 models reveal an emergent phenomenon: geometric latent reasoning induces substantially shorter generations without an explicit length objective. By replacing early explicit reasoning with continuous latent steps, models often reach correct answers using substantially fewer total generation steps. These findings suggest that continuous trajectories act as compact intermediate reasoning states, exposing a new tradeoff between latent computation budget, output length, and accuracy. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/idiap/GLR. The project page is available at: https://glr-llm.github.io/.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: TrajLift: Lifting Memory Recall Trajectories with Latency-Modulated Heat Diffusion
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Verbal memory retrieval carries rich diagnostic information for Alzheimer's disease through the order, hesitation, and categorical organization of recalled words, yet computational modeling of this retrieval process remains largely unexplored. A key challenge is that timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled: the diagnostic meaning of retrieval timing depends on its hierarchical context. We propose TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a hierarchical graph. Our central mechanism is latency-modulated heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy, a unified operator that lifts each recalled word into a representation of both multi-scale hierarchical structure and continuous retrieval timing. Formal analysis shows that the resulting representation is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchical levels. On synthetic benchmarks requiring structure-time interaction, TrajLift stays near-perfect on deep hierarchies where all baselines fail. On real-world clinical data, we show that TrajLift outperforms diverse baselines by jointly modeling timing and semantic structure, with gains that grow as retrieval timing becomes more informative.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: MAAM: Anchor-Preserving Compression and Contextual Calibration for Chinese Discriminatory Language Detection
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Chinese discriminatory-language detection is challenging because harmful intent is often implicit and context-dependent. We propose MAAM (Myopia--Astigmatism Anchor Mechanism), a lightweight, model-agnostic framework inspired by functional visual blur: rather than preserving every token equally, MAAM retains discrimination-relevant semantic anchors and calibrates them with C--I--S contextual priors (Contextual Tone, Group Identity, and Stance Polarity). Compared with frontier LLM baselines under zero-shot and few-shot prompting protocols, MAAM remains competitive while offering stronger compactness and stability. These results suggest that interpretable anchor preservation and contextual calibration provide a practical alternative to heavier model scaling for Chinese discriminatory-language assessment.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: VEX-Bench: Benchmarking Verification Complexity of LLM-Generated Misinformation
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have made misinformation inexpensive to produce but not to verify, creating a growing asymmetry in the information ecosystem. Under tight time, labor, and budget constraints, media organizations, platforms, and fact-checkers rely on screening to prioritize which content to verify. We introduce VEX-Bench, a unified benchmark for evaluating the verification complexity of LLM-generated misinformation, as perceived during screening, across models and generation methods. Verification complexity is assessed along multiple dimensions derived from journalistic and fact-checking practices, capturing checkability, harm potential, source credibility signals, imposter legitimacy, and expected verification effort. We define the VEX score as an integrated measure combining elicitation yield and verification complexity to quantify how generated content consumes limited verification capacity. We construct a benchmark spanning two misinformation categories, 6 high-stakes domains, and 60 real-world topics, and evaluate 7 frontier LLMs and 7 generation methods, yielding 5{,}880 articles. We employ an LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation and validate it using content-analysis methodology, including ordinal Krippendorff $α$ for inter-annotator reliability, complemented by fact-checking agents for verification. Our findings show that no single method dominates all dimensions, underscoring the need for multi-dimensional evaluation. LLMs can generate high-VEX misinformation at 3$\times$ to 169$\times$ lower cost than agent-based verification. Such content is often prioritized during screening, consuming scarce verification resources and introducing a systematic risk of misallocation in resource-constrained verification systems. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: An Enigma of Artificial Reason: Investigating the Production-Evaluation Gap in Large Reasoning Models
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary:
Studies of human reasoning have shown that people are typically stronger at evaluating reasoning than producing it from scratch. In contrast, large reasoning models (LRMs) are trained to excel at producing long chains of reasoning to solve complex problems. How then do LRMs perform at evaluating reasons? We investigate this with the Valid-Answer-Invalid-Reasoning (VAIR) dataset: math problems and solutions with trivial reasoning flaws but valid answers, designed to isolate reasoning evaluation from the confound of reasoning production. Unlike humans, who we find are only 6% worse at grading than solving such problems, we find a substantial production-evaluation gap in LRMs: frontier models score as low as 52% when evaluating VAIR solutions, despite near-perfect solution production.
  Why this enigma? Through chain-of-thought (CoT) analysis, we find evidence of an answer confirmation bias: LRMs often produce then check for the correct answer instead of carefully verifying each step, fabricating rationalizations even when noticing anomalous reasoning. Linear probes corroborate this, showing that while LRM activations encode some representation of valid reasoning, they fail to robustly represent VAIR solutions as invalid. Causal patching of the final answer's representations causes LRM verdicts and activations to flip at substantial rates, demonstrating that answer validity is a causal factor in models' confirmation biases. These findings indicate an outstanding limitation in dominant approaches to reasoning training, which incentivize LRMs to produce and confirm reasoning towards correct answers, but not to robustly evaluate the underlying reasons

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Adaptive Entropy-Sparing for Efficient Reasoning
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) produce explicit chains of thought to improve transparency, but they frequently overthink, generating long yet inefficient reasoning chains that inflate computational costs and risk introducing errors. While numerous reinforcement learning methods struggle to penalize verbosity to achieve conciseness, they typically apply the penalty uniformly across lengthy sequences, which leads to credit confounding, that is, the failure to distinguish essential reasoning steps from superfluous ones. In this paper, we study a measurable proxy for this confounding: high-entropy tokens that often coincide with surface transition points where reasoning re-enters verification. Based on this insight, we propose Adaptive Entropy-Sparing (AES), which selectively spares high-entropy tokens that occur before an efficient in-group reference, while penalizing overlength high-entropy suffix tokens associated with superfluous branching. Our AES thereby navigates the suppression-exploration trade-off, reducing overthinking while preserving average reasoning accuracy. We also present an entropy-length model that motivates why local uncertainty can serve as a proxy for future reasoning cost. Across eight reasoning benchmarks, AES reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% while increasing mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over the base models, consistently outperforming existing efficiency-oriented methods. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Pause and Reflect: Conformal Aggregation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with self-consistency improves performance by aggregating multiple sampled reasoning paths. In this setting, correctness is no longer tied to a single reasoning trace but to the aggregation rule over a pool of candidate paths, making aggregation uncertainty the central challenge. This issue is critical where confidently incorrect answers are far more costly than abstentions. We introduce a conformal procedure for CoT reasoning that directly addresses aggregation uncertainty. Our approach replaces majority voting with weighted score aggregation over reasoning paths and calibrates an abstention rule using conformal risk control. This approach leads to finite-sample guarantees on the confident-error rate--the probability that the system answers and is wrong. We further identify score separability as the key condition under which abstention provably improves selective accuracy, and derive closed-form expressions that predict accuracy gains from calibration data alone. The method is fully inference-time, and requires no retraining. Across four benchmarks, four open-source models, and three score classes, realized confident-error rates are consistent with the prescribed targets up to calibration-split and test-set variability. Our method achieves $90.1\%$ selective accuracy on GSM8K by abstaining on fewer than $5\%$ of problems, compared with $82.3\%$ accuracy under majority voting and $87.4\%$ under score-weighted voting without abstention, while conformal risk control keeps the expected rate of confidently wrong answers below $10\%$.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: DynEdit: Dynamic Entropy-Guided Sequential Editing for Large Language Models
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated or incorrect knowledge in large language models without full retraining. In this work, we show that token entropy is closely associated with both editing difficulty and semantic importance: high-entropy regions are harder to edit and often contain key factual content. DynEdit uses token-level entropy to guide non-uniform sliding, increasing the coverage of difficult high-entropy regions, and further applies entropy-guided token-level optimization to strengthen updates on information-dense tokens within each editing window. Experiments on three benchmarks and two backbone models show that DynEdit consistently outperforms competitive baselines across diverse long-form editing settings, achieving gains of up to +14.0 BLEU points on challenging paraphrase queries and near-saturated semantic scores on several diverse knowledge domains.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: GLINT: Sparsely Gated Vision-Language Alignment for Fine-Grained Radiology Representations
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) for radiology have emerged as a scalable paradigm by leveraging image-report pairs naturally produced in clinical workflows. However, this pairing reveals a mismatch in scale: each finding occupies only a small region of the image, yet supervision is provided only at the global image-report level. To address this, we present GLINT (Gated Language-Image alignmeNT), a framework that models this sparse correspondence. On the alignment side, we introduce Sparsely Gated Alignment, a novel architecture in which a sigmoid gate over a separate gate embedding space activates only the patches relevant to each textual query, yielding sparsity. On the representation side, we add Dense Feature Regularization, which anchors the trainable encoder's intermediate features to a frozen self-supervised learning (SSL) teacher, preserving the fine-grained patch features that the gate relies on. GLINT enables zero-shot classification, grounding, and segmentation from free-text queries, and to our knowledge is the first to demonstrate zero-shot segmentation on 3D CT volumes without mask supervision. Notably, the most pronounced gains arise on zero-shot grounding and segmentation, where sparse, query-specific localization is required, consistent with our design intent. In downstream evaluation, GLINT outperforms both SSL encoders and medical VLMs on classification, report generation, and segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/deepnoid-ai/GLINT.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Measuring Definition Sensitivity in LLM Annotation of Social Science Concepts
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: In social science research, text annotation is a fundamental task that is traditionally a costly, hard-to-scale manual process. Researchers have used large language models (LLMs) to perform annotation by writing a definition of a concept into a prompt - a rule that determines whether a label should be attributed to a text depending on its content. However, concepts such as hate speech, fake news, and terrorism typically have several theoretically defensible competing definitions. It is also unknown whether the model actually applied the definition to provide the label or the label was based on the model's pretrained notion of the concept. To test this, we have the model annotate the same texts twice, each time with a different definition. We call the disagreement between the two sets of annotations definition sensitivity. As a control, we paraphrase one definition but leave its requirements unchanged - the disagreement between the annotations with the two wordings becomes the paraphrase floor. Across six concepts and three LLMs, a swap of competing definitions always changes more annotations, on average, than a paraphrase. This shows that the annotations depend on the prompted definition, so any set of annotations should be interpreted together with the definition that produced it. The LLM annotator's definition sensitivity and its paraphrase floor should both be reported in such work.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Self-Modeling Interventions can Modulate Emergent Misalignment
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Emergent misalignment (EM) has been linked to the activation of misaligned persona vectors and evil character traits, suggesting that EM operates through disruption of the model's aligned character rather than direct learning of harmful content. Motivated by this connection, we study self-modeling interventions: specifically self-recognition and self-reports as character-targeted interventions that are distinct from existing in-training defenses. We conduct two-stage finetuning experiments across three models (GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct) and multiple EM datasets to compare self-recognition finetuning against benign finetuning baselines (correct domain-specific data, general knowledge, and word counting), finding it an effective defense in both reversal and prevention settings. For prevention, only self-recognition finetuning consistently reduces misalignment without exacerbating any individual metric, suggesting that character fortification specifically drives prevention. We also conduct in-training experiments across these models to compare the effectiveness of self-reports with benign interleaving and inoculation prompting. We provide further evidence for EM's relation to the LLM's default character by showing that EM finetuning leads to fragmentation of LLM's identity self-reports, reduces self-recognition performance to about chance, artificially corrupting self-recognition exacerbates misalignment caused by EM finetuning, and finetuning on self-reports from EM finetuned models can transfer misalignment. Together, these findings reframe EM not as the adoption of a coherent misaligned persona but as the destabilization of aligned character.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Semantic Motion Anchors: Bridging Motion and Meaning in Co-Speech Gestures
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Learning a shared representation between spoken text and gesture is central to co-speech gesture retrieval, synthesis, and understanding, but remains challenging for semantically meaningful gestures whose communicative intent is not captured by motion alone. Direct contrastive alignment between transcripts and continuous motion embeddings often overemphasizes low-level kinematics and misses the symbolic content of semantic gestures. We propose semantic motion anchors, natural-language abstractions of gesture motion capturing physical form and communicative intent. Our method discretizes 3D gestures into body-hand motion primitives, verbalizes them into structured descriptions, and grounds them in the transcript to provide auxiliary contrastive supervision. On BEAT2, our method improves text-to-gesture R@1 by 8.2% over a direct text-motion baseline and outperforms prior retrieval approaches on text to gesture and gesture to text retrieval directions. Beyond aggregate retrieval metrics, semantic motion anchor supervision helps retrieve gestures that are semantically meaningful for the spoken query, rather than defaulting to generic motion patterns. A downstream retrieval-augmented gesture generation study showed that users significantly preferred gestures retrieved by our approach over a retrieval-augmented generation baseline, demonstrating that semantically grounded retrieval translates to gestures that better convey communicative intent in downstream generation.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Hidden Measurement Error in LLM Pipelines Distorts Annotation, Evaluation, and Benchmarking
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: LLM evaluations drive model deployment, safety standards, research conclusions, and future projections, for example, about AI's impact on the labor market. Yet the way we often estimate noise from autoraters (LLM-as-judge) ignores variability from factors like judge model choice and prompt phrasing, which means we're underestimating error in a way that worsens with more data. This unmeasured variance can affect results enough to reverse conclusions. And judge-pipelines that fail to average this variation are more vulnerable to "benchmark hacking". This paper introduces a framework we call "total evaluation error (TEE)," which decomposes LLM pipeline uncertainty and uses design-study projections to reduce total error. In our safety and ideology applications, naive standard errors are 53-70% smaller than the corrected SE under our TEE framework. Using Chatbot Arena data, we show naive 95% CI coverage drops as n grows, while TEE-corrected coverage holds at 95%, and TEE-guided pipelines restrict the potential range of benchmark gaming by roughly 43%. We show further that a small pilot allows for the estimation of proper CIs, with the added benefit of projecting which design changes most improve precision. Using those projections to allocate API calls cut MMLU estimation error roughly in half against the answer key at the same budget, and increased per-match agreement with human voters on Chatbot Arena by 7.9 percentage points.
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 14 pages, 7 figures. SI Appendix: https://solomonmg.github.io/pdf/totalevalerror_si.pdf

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: One Temperature to Rule Them All?
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Inference-time sampling is a central mechanism for improving large language models, with temperature controlling the tradeoff between reliability and diversity. While recent work suggests that varying temperature across samples can improve multi-sample inference, simple fixed-temperature schemes remain the standard in practice. We investigate this discrepancy in the canonical pass@K setting, asking when temperature diversity is useful, and when a single tuned temperature suffices. To this end, we analyze per-question success probabilities across multiple models and datasets, tracking how they vary with sampling temperature. We identify several consistent properties of these profiles, including that harder questions are less likely to share efficient sampling temperatures, although this trend is only logarithmic in hardness. We then derive an efficient method for evaluating the theoretically optimal multi-temperature allocation scheme, and show that although such a scheme improves performance, its gains over single-temperature baselines are typically modest when temperature is tuned as a function of the sampling budget K. We explain this phenomenon through mathematical mechanisms that we call dulling effects, and show how they ensure the robustness of temperature choices across different question distributions. Our results clarify when multi-temperature sampling is useful, and how temperatures should ideally be chosen.

Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. \textsc{NarrativeBench} provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.

Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.title: Scaling Taxonomy-Free Image Labeling with Generative AI: A Multimodal
Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.summary:
Providing real-time multimodal insights into images is challenging because it requires low latency, high description accuracy, and scalable solutions that are both cost-effective and efficient. For example, given a new image of an outfit, we would like to generate insights that the image depicts "earth tones" and "linen pants" and allow users to explore similar ideas along these themes. Traditional strategies to generate such insights would typically involve building taxonomies producing a golden set labeled by humans, training models on these datasets, and deploying these models for online inference services. Such workflows are constrained by fixed taxonomy, high labeling cost, limited labeling coverage in sample space, and human errors and expertise gaps in labelers. In addition, these methods are expensive and cumbersome to iterate over time. Recent trends have started exploring generative AI models for online insights, but this method suffers from long latency and prohibitive costs to support a high volume of requests or large amounts of offline labeling needs.
  We present Generative Labeling On Clusters (GLOC) as a solution to provide highly scalable, cost-effective, low latency, and high accuracy online image insight services. GLOC leverages highly optimized image embeddings to form image clusters that are semantically close to each other for the purpose of the type of insights, and summarizes the insights at the cluster level, which effectively generalizes to members in the cluster. At Pinterest, GLOC powers image descriptors and pivot query suggestions for Hybrid Search, which is a multimodal search service enabling users to search with both an image and a text query. Our offline and online A/B tests demonstrate that GLOC significantly outperforms previous methods, delivering improvements in quality and efficiency.
