Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Sophon: A Procedural Diagnostic for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Open-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) score 85-94% on spatial benchmarks (BLINK Spatial, What's Up CLEVR) yet collapse to chance on simple geometric questions when object, scene, and texture priors are stripped away. We introduce and open-source Sophon, a procedurally generated diagnostic of paired colored point-cloud stimuli across three coordinate systems (1D linear, 2D Cartesian, 2D polar) and four question types (binary, categorical, comparative, quantitative). Across four open architectures (LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2.5-VL, Idefics3), accuracy clusters at 47-52% while frontier models (Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4) clear 77-83% and humans reach 84-94%. We use linear probes and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to trace the open-weight failures. Probes of the vision encoder (ViT) and language decoder (LLM) recover Sophon spatial information at 83-85% and 80-86% accuracy, respectively, and the language tower's reasoning circuit answers text-only controls (point clouds as sets of coordinates) at +40 pp over visual stimuli. Language tower per-layer attention attribution localizes visual integration to mid-stack layers. At readout, models elevate the correct answer-set tokens but select among them randomly. We localize the mechanism by tuning individual and grouped components across every architecture's stack, including the vision tower (ViT workspace and reader), the projector, and the language tower (LLM workspace and reader). These experiments demonstrate that this mid-stack workspace holds circuitry capable of organizing the spatial signal so that the frozen reader can decode it. LoRA fine-tuning adjusts that circuitry such that 7B-class VLMs answer Sophon spatial reasoning questions at frontier aggregate accuracy. This work suggests that these models do not have a capability gap for spatial reasoning but suffer from a routing bottleneck that targeted fine-tuning repairs.
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).comment: NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). 10 page main text, 44 pages total. Code and data: https://github.com/zgazak/sophon

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: The Dynamic-Probabilistic Consistency Gap in Chaotic Surrogate Modeling
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Dynamical systems reconstruction (DSR) aims to learn surrogate models that capture the dynamics underlying time-series data. Reliable scientific inference with these surrogates requires uncertainty estimates consistent with the learned dynamics. We expose a dynamic-probabilistic consistency (DPC) gap: optimizing finite-horizon probabilistic objectives can degrade the learned dynamics or decouple predictive uncertainty from the local tangent dynamics it should reflect. We isolate three mechanisms behind this gap: core collapse, noise masking, and blind uncertainty. Specifically, we show that open-loop rollout objectives can penalize covariance growth driven by the dynamics, encouraging optimization shortcuts that weaken local expansion. To mitigate this gap, we propose KAFFEE (Kalman-Aware Framework For Ergodic Emulation), a differentiable extended Kalman filter-based training framework that jointly learns dynamics and noise covariances by coupling filtered innovation likelihoods with covariance propagation through learned local Jacobians, while differentiating through the Kalman updates. On stochastic hyperchaotic Lorenz-96, KAFFEE mitigates the identified failure modes and improves both reconstruction of dynamical invariants and predictive scores relative to open-loop objectives. The DPC gap also appears when probabilistically adapting a DSR foundation model across 13 chaotic systems, where KAFFEE improves predictive likelihood over open-loop adaptation while preserving the pretrained model's long-term dynamics and enabling in-context Bayesian filtering.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: LOFT: Low-Rank Orthogonal Fine-Tuning via Task-Aware Support Selection
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Orthogonal parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts pretrained weights through structure-preserving multiplicative transformations, but existing methods often conflate two distinct design choices: the subspace in which adaptation occurs and the transformation applied within that subspace. This paper introduces LOFT, a low-rank orthogonal fine-tuning framework that explicitly separates these two components. By viewing orthogonal adaptation as a multiplicative subspace rotation, LOFT provides a unified formulation that recovers the multiplicative core of representative orthogonal PEFT methods, including coordinate-, butterfly-, Householder- (with a learnable support) and principal-subspace-based variants (up to scaling and relaxation). More importantly, this perspective exposes support selection as a central design axis rather than a byproduct of a particular parameterization. We develop a first-order analysis showing that useful adaptation supports should be informed by the downstream training signal, motivating practical task-aware support selection strategies. Across language understanding, visual transfer, mathematical reasoning, and multilingual out-of-distribution adaptation, LOFT with task-aware supports improves performance at matched trainable-parameter and transform settings under a shared protocol. This suggests that, under a fixed transform and budget, the choice of support affects performance, making systematic support selection an important direction for improving orthogonal PEFT.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared with the verifier's pooled 87.6% (paired difference: +4.8 points, 95% interval [-8.2, 18.5]). A diagnostic sample reveals a distinct failure mode: 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction without ever reaching a judge. Finally, external-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%, compared with 87.6% answer-key match. These audits lack human or formal-kernel ground truth. Open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement, which measures consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth. These results motivate separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity. We provide per-configuration results and evaluation details in the supplement.
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 13 tables. Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI) at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/yashica-patodia/certify-or-decline

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: When Graph Structure Provably Helps Classification: Non-Asymptotic Recovery Guarantees
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: The joint use of graph structure and node-specific information is central to transductive node classification, yet a fundamental theoretical question remains: when does graph structure actually help? We provide the first deterministic, non-asymptotic, distribution-free answer to this question. We build on nuclear-norm graph clustering and generalized convex clustering. Our formulation of the latter incorporates node features, partial labels, and general convex loss functions, making it suitable for transductive node classification. We analyze each problem separately to characterize when graph structure alone, or node information alone, is sufficient for perfect recovery. We then formulate a unified convex optimization problem through a shared atomic norm representation and prove that combining the two sources expands the range of conditions under which perfect recovery is guaranteed beyond what either source alone can certify. This shows when node information can improve clustering and graph structure can improve classification.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Reward-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Sample-efficient reinforcement learning typically uses a fixed reward function both to guide exploration and to supervise learning. However, the same experience can provide supervision under multiple related reward specifications, even when the objective of interest remains fixed. We introduce Reward-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (RCRL), an off-policy approach that collects experience under a nominal objective while training a reward-conditioned agent using counterfactual rewards recomputed from replay. RCRL constructs alternative reward specifications by perturbing the nominal reward, providing diverse supervision without additional environment interaction. Across single-task, multi-task, and vision-based control benchmarks, RCRL improves nominal task performance and sample efficiency when integrated with strong RL backbones. As a secondary capability, the learned policies support zero-shot behavioral adjustment toward related objectives without further training. These results demonstrate that diverse reward supervision can improve learning of a predefined objective while also enabling policy steerability.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Joint Learning of Hierarchical Neural Options and Abstract World Model
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Building agents that can perform new skills by composing existing skills is a long-standing goal of AI agent research. Towards this end, we investigate how to efficiently acquire a sequence of skills, formalized as hierarchical neural options. However, existing model-free hierarchical reinforcement algorithms need a lot of data. We propose a novel method, which we call AgentOWL (Option and World model Learning Agent), that jointly learns -- in a sample efficient way -- an abstract world model (abstracting across both states and time) and a set of hierarchical neural options. We show, on a subset of Object-Centric Atari games, that our method can learn more skills using less data than baseline methods and possesses learning and generalization capabilities that the baselines do not have.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Graph Label Alignment: A Diagnostic Atlas for Graph Classification
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Graph classification benchmarks vary widely in difficulty: some are solved by simple pooled baselines, while others remain challenging for GNNs and graph transformers. We take a data-centric view and ask whether benchmark success is driven by genuine structure--feature reasoning or by label signal already accessible from restricted marginal views. We introduce graph label alignment, a lightweight diagnostic that measures label accessibility through two supervised probes computed without training a graph encoder: structural label alignment (SLA), based on permutation-invariant topological and spectral summaries, and feature label alignment (FLA), based on pooled node features with edges removed. Across real graph classification benchmarks and multiple pooled backbones, the resulting SLA--FLA plane strongly organizes test accuracy, with low-alignment datasets forming a consistent regime where standard pooled pipelines struggle. To probe what lies beyond marginal accessibility, we introduce controlled interaction-dominated stress tests, including heterophilic ego-graphs and synthetic Twins tasks whose structural and feature marginals are matched across classes but whose role--feature couplings differ. These results show that high alignment explains much of easy benchmark performance, while low alignment reveals regimes where success requires preserving structure--feature correspondence beyond standard pooled representations.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Visual Instruction Tuning Aligns Modalities through Abstraction
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Visual instruction tuning effectively adapts a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) to process image information alongside text. Yet it remains unclear how visual features are embedded within the layer-wise hierarchy of abstractions in the LLM backbone. Across a diverse set of vision-language architectures, we show that instruction tuning primarily serves as a bridge, embedding visual features directly into the intermediate semantic layers of the LLM, bypassing the early layers devoted to unimodal processing. With probing analyses and causal interventions, we show that these intermediate layers constitute the semantic core of vision-language processing and play a critical role in performance across a broad set of multimodal benchmarks. In addition, by comparing the geometry of semantically equivalent visual and textual representations, we find that fine-tuning extends and strengthens the existing abstraction phase, aligning visual features with pre-existing textual ones. Finally, we confirm the functional role of this localized alignment by restricting fine-tuning to intermediate layers alone: this strategy preserves the performance of full fine-tuning on vision-centric benchmarks while reducing training time. Our results suggest that multimodal integration is a localized phenomenon driven by the repurposing of the internal abstraction engine of the LLM.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: From Nodes to Pixels: Topological and Structural Two-View Graph Imaging
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Graph learning still lacks a broadly reusable input interface comparable to patches in vision or tokens in language. Unlike images or text, graphs are irregular, vary in size and density, and are invariant under many equivalent node labelings, making it difficult to standardize inputs across tasks and architectures. We introduce G2Image, a fixed-budget graph imaging framework that converts each graph into two complementary image-like views. TopoGrid provides a stable topological view by encoding an intrinsic bifiltration as a compact multipersistence surface grid, while GraphGrid provides a higher-bandwidth structural view by aggregating edge densities between groups defined by intrinsic node scores. Both views are permutation-invariant and come with resolution-controlled stability guarantees. Because the resulting representations are fixed-size tensors, they can be processed by lightweight 2D encoders and aligned through a supervised cross-view contrastive objective. Across graph classification and molecular prediction benchmarks, G2Image achieves strong average performance among the compared methods, improves over single-view and standard fusion variants, and extends to attribute-rich molecular graphs without changing the overall architecture. These results suggest that fixed-budget graph images offer a practical and reusable interface for graph representation learning.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Don't Match the Noise: Distribution Matching under Unknown Measurement Error with an Audit Sample
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Real-world machine learning systems often operate on imperfect measurements: sensors are noisy, annotations are produced by non-experts, and scientific observations are often indirect. In these settings, classic distribution comparison tools such as maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) can be systematically biased, matching artifacts of the measurement process rather than the underlying mechanisms of interest. We study a practical regime in which noisy observations are abundant, but only a small audited subset contains ground-truth measurements. We propose measurement-error-corrected MMD (MEC-MMD), an audit-based estimator that debiases kernel evaluations without requiring a noise model. MEC-MMD is exactly unbiased for the oracle MMD under simple random auditing, admits an explicit variance decomposition, and is consistent for the population MMD, achieving the standard $O_p(N^{-1/2})$ rate when the audit size scales with the dataset. We demonstrate the utility of distributional matching with MEC-MMD loss for both parameter estimation and unsupervised applications, showing that MEC-MMD consistently outperforms MMD and alternative methods. These results provide a principled foundation for robust distribution comparison, simulation-based inference, and learning in noisy real-world machine learning pipelines.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: A New Framework for Quantum Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) has emerged as a promising approach for controlling quantum systems and accelerating learning tasks with quantum resources. However, most existing QRL formulations still retain a classical reinforcement learning interface: states and actions are often encoded in computational bases and rewards are extracted through measurements. This interface is restrictive for genuinely quantum environments: choosing a measurement can discard entanglement information, while repeated intermediate measurements collapse the evolving state and require costly re-preparation. This motivates a fully QRL framework in which the agent, environment, rewards, and return accumulation are all quantum. In this paper, we take a step toward this goal and introduce a new QRL framework in which both the policy and the environment are modeled by conditional quantum channels. We then propose a quantum policy-gradient algorithm for parameterized conditional quantum channels with a trainable control basis. We also derive finite- and infinite-horizon gradient estimators using a new parameter-shift rule. This rule is needed because policy parameters are shared across repeated interaction blocks and the infinite-horizon objective is not a finite circuit; rather than shifting every occurrence and evaluating the whole trajectory, our estimator shifts only one sampled policy block. Sampling this block from a geometric distribution yields an unbiased gradient estimator under bounded rewards. Finally, we establish convergence of the resulting stochastic gradient-ascent procedure to stationary points under standard smoothness and step-size assumptions.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Quantitative Assessment of Crystal Structure Prediction
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) aims to predict a material's 3D structure from its chemical composition, with applications from energy storage to biomedical devices. Despite its importance, existing evaluation frameworks suffer from key limitations: they rely on threshold-sensitive or incomparable metrics, focus predominantly on geometric performance while overlooking physical plausibility, and fail to account for polymorphism, where a chemical composition can crystallize into multiple stable structures. In parallel, recent Symmetry-Informed CSP (SICSP) methods often report results alongside standard CSP baselines while receiving crystallographic templates at inference, which constrain the search space and make SICSP a fundamentally different task. To address these limitations, we introduce an Orientation-invariant, Polymorph-Aware, Large Benchmark (OPAL-Bench) that evaluates CSP and SICSP as separate tasks. We evaluate 7 CSP and 2 SICSP methods under OPAL-Bench across 4 datasets using threshold-free geometric and physical distance metrics. Our results show that no method dominates across all metrics, and that geometric performance is not strongly correlated with physical plausibility. We also release OPAL-CSP, an SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching baseline for the CSP track that performs competitively on geometric metrics and ranks among the best on physical ones. By unifying geometric and physical metrics under a polymorph-aware protocol, OPAL-Bench enables a more comprehensive assessment of generative quality in CSP.
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 49 pages, 21 figures, 17 tables. Code: https://github.com/BCV-Uniandes/OPAL

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. We propose {code explanations to address the mismatch in how LLM explanations are generated versus how they are evaluated: a program explains LLM behavior across a dataset of inputs, and its execution enables automatic verification. We define Consistency metric that measures the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs, and use it to evaluate and select candidate programs. Across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks, we find that LLMs can produce highly consistent code explanations in several settings. Code explanations are also 6$\times$ to 100$\times$ shorter than CoT, and better align with model behavior in 9 out of 24 settings. However, consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where generated programs reproduce model outputs no more frequently than an uninformative explanation baseline, and these programs often rely on longer hard-coded patterns. In experiments with Claude Opus 5.5, providing the model with consistency feedback and code execution improves explanation consistency across tasks, but consistency remains significantly lower on more complex tasks. Our findings establish executable code as a novel, verifiable, and compact approach to explaining LLM behavior and highlight verification feedback as a promising direction for improving explanation consistency. The code for this paper is at https://github.com/rajesh-lab/code-as-explanations.
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).comment: 30 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables, The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: MotionCFG: Boosting Motion Dynamics via Semantic Motion Sharpening
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Despite recent advancements in Text-to-Video (T2V) synthesis, generating high-fidelity and dynamic motion remains a significant challenge. Existing methods primarily rely on Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG), but standard CFG treats all semantic dimensions uniformly and provides no mechanism to selectively resolve ambiguity along the motion axis. To address this, we propose MotionCFG, a training-free approach that introduces selective guidance along the motion subspace of the condition embedding. Specifically, we construct a motion-perturbed negative condition by injecting Gaussian noise into motion-related embeddings, and steer generation away from it to selectively amplify motion intent. We show theoretically that this procedure implicitly approximates Semantic Laplacian Sharpening, a second-order correction that suppresses motion-ambiguous regions of the score landscape and amplifies well-resolved dynamic peaks. Combined with a piecewise guidance schedule that confines intervention to the early denoising steps, MotionCFG consistently improves motion dynamics across state-of-the-art T2V frameworks with negligible overhead. We further demonstrate that this Laplacian sharpening principle generalizes beyond motion, effectively steering complex, non-linear concepts such as precise object numerosity that are typically difficult to modulate via standard text-based guidance. Our project page is available at https://motion-cfg.vercel.app/.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Where Should the Code Go? Locating Foundation-Model Errors in Bitemporal Inventory Simulation
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Operational reports carry two clocks: when an event happened and when its report arrived; later reports can revise earlier ones. A foundation-model component that maintains the state supported by the reports visible at a cutoff, then rolls a supplied scenario forward, can be helped by exact code before it, after it or inside the call, or asked to reason harder. We ask which remedy removes which error, for which models, on an exactly solvable lost-sales inventory environment: 36,672 independently rescored requests over twelve configurations of closed and open-weight models, with a forced-answer-call interface as a control and protocols frozen before the calls. Weak models fail in separable ways. Canonical input removes report-selection error, exact continuation removes rollout error, neither repairs the other, and which error dominates differs by model; strong models are at ceiling on raw reports. Asking for more reasoning is no substitute and can depend on the interface: under a forced answer call high effort collapses GPT-5.4 mini and DeepSeek V4 Pro, which gain or hold under automatic choice; on its provider the forced call disables reasoning for DeepSeek V4 Flash; and at high effort gpt-oss exhausts its output budget. The contribution is a controlled component diagnostic, released with every request, and evidence that for some model and provider pairs the tool-calling interface confounds reasoning evaluation.
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).comment: 22 pages. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems (FMTS). Code and data: https://github.com/durga-sandeep/where-should-the-code-go

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Certification from Examples is Hard for Circuits and Transformers under Minimal Overparametrization
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: As state-of-the-art neural networks are deployed on reasoning and algorithmic tasks, exactness guarantees become increasingly important. However, high average-case accuracy can still mask incorrect behaviors. This motivates exact certification, which asks for the smallest set of labeled examples needed to certify that a learned hypothesis equals the target. We show that while some hypotheses are easy to certify, even minimal overparametrization can make certification exponentially hard across several hypothesis classes. For threshold circuits of depth $\ge 2$, adding a single extra gate can force certificate sizes exponential in the input dimension. We show an analogous hardness result for log-precision Transformers with only constant architectural overhead. We also characterize approximate certification, showing that allowing only polynomially many mistakes still requires exponentially large certificates, whereas constant relative-error guarantees can hide exponentially many failures. Empirically, we study binary-addition recognition using threshold circuits and Transformers trained with strong supervision. We find that incorrect models can survive extensive checks, with errors that often occur on different inputs and are difficult to detect through uniform sampling.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Closing the Loop: Co-Evolving EM for Irregular Time Series Generation in Lifted Representations
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Regular time-series generation from irregular time series is typically reduced to one-shot imputation: complete each partial sequence once, freeze the completions, and train a generator on the resulting surrogate dataset. We show that this open-loop strategy is structurally flawed. Point imputers collapse ambiguous missing regions to conditional averages, while stochastic imputers become stale as the generator evolves; the binding constraint is therefore iteration, not imputer design. We introduce a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework that closes the imputer-generator loop. Each E-step samples missing values from the posterior of the current generator, and each M-step retrains the generator on these completions, preserving unconditional generator training. Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Incremental Learning of Sparse Attention Patterns in Transformers
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Transformers integrate information from multiple past positions through sparse attention patterns that copy from specific locations. We study how these patterns form during training in a high-order Markov-chain setting, where the next token depends on several groups of past positions with differing statistical importance. Learning proceeds in discrete stages, each marked by the emergence of a sparse attention pattern for the next most important group. The dynamics are initially competitive, with all attention heads focusing on the dominant pattern, but later become cooperative, with different heads specializing in distinct patterns. For a tractable surrogate, the dynamics reduce to those of a tensor factorization problem, enabling us to prove stagewise convergence. Empirically, the number of stages completed depends on training set size, suggesting a form of implicit complexity control through early stopping. Overall, we give a theoretical account of how structured attention patterns and head specialization emerge without an explicit curriculum.

Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).title: Adversarial Risk in the Generative AI Era Necessitates Dropping the Small Epsilon Ball
Machine Learning (Top Venues & Labs).summary: Adversarial Machine Learning research is currently centered on the search for the epsilon-ball: minimal perturbations designed to fool models while remaining imperceptible to humans. We argue that this fixation on $\ell_p$ norms is a metrological trap that communicates a distorted perception of risk to defenders, one that is unaligned with real-world system vulnerabilities. This paradigm misleads defenders into optimizing for narrow, mathematical robustness at the expense of systemic security, while simultaneously incentivizing attackers to exploit non-overlapping alternative adversarial pathways. Ultimately, we argue that the dominance of the $\ell_p$ ball does not just fail to reduce harm---it may actively facilitate it by communicating a false sense of security against the wrong threats.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong visual understanding, yet the internal features that cause these behaviors remain difficult to identify, audit, or control. MMDiff supports three uses: (i) feature isolation, by diffing a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart to identify features altered by multimodal training; (ii) task-specific feature detection, via per-token contrastive firing analysis that isolates causal features; and (iii) feature-level control, by causally removing or steering the discovered feature directions. MMDiff discovers sparse, causally specific features whose removal selectively degrades target behaviors by an average of 12% on spatial tasks and 17% on OCR, and reduces attack success rate by 24% on multimodal safety attacks, with no impact on VQA performance. Steering these features improves spatial and OCR accuracy by +3.6% and +1.8% on average over a standard single-layer steering baseline. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Building Comparative Motivation Profiles with Symmetric Belief Editing
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: When a model behaves in unexpected ways, we want to know why, but its intent cannot be observed directly, and its self-reports may be rationalizations. We introduce comparative motivation profiles, which treat intent as propensity: we edit the model's beliefs about facts that a hypothesized motivation would depend on and measure how its behavior changes. To keep artifacts of the editing method from driving the result, we edit two minimally different hypotheses in the same way, with matched amplify and suppress edits; we call this symmetric belief editing. We apply it to alignment faking in four open-weight model organisms, contrasting scheming, which tracks the training consequences of compliance, with performative misalignment, which tracks what researchers expect to observe, and edit beliefs with synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF), activation steering, and prompting. Under SDF, amplifying performative beliefs raises alignment faking on every model, while scheming edits move it less or shift compliance in the monitored and unmonitored conditions alike. Steering on model organisms changes compliance along the expectation-tracking direction but mainly the reasoning along the consequence-tracking direction, and prompting agrees. In these organisms, alignment faking follows what the models infer their evaluators expect, which puts it closer to sycophancy than to deceptive alignment.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: AI-Mediated Communication Can Steer Collective Opinion
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into the online platforms where humans exchange opinions; large language models (LLMs) have been polishing users' posts on LinkedIn and providing context for content shared on X. While prior work has shown that AI can express biased opinions and shape individuals' opinions during human-AI interactions, less attention has been paid to its influence on collective opinion formation when mediating human-to-human communication. We show empirically that LLMs from multiple popular families introduce directional biases when instructed to edit human-written texts on contested topics, for example, nudging texts in favor of gun control and against atheism. By analytically characterizing the equilibrium of this model and performing simulations on real social network data, we show that biases introduced by AI in human-to-human communication can be amplified through the network and shift collective opinion in their direction. In light of these findings, we investigate whether such biases are controllable by online platforms. We audit the "Explain this post" feature on X and find evidence of pro-life bias in Grok's outputs on abortion-related content, which we trace back to specific design choices. We conclude with a discussion of the broader implications of our findings in relation to ongoing legislative efforts in the European Union.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: GSQ: Highly-Accurate Low-Precision Scalar Quantization for LLMs via Gumbel-Softmax Sampling
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Quantization has become a standard tool for efficient LLM deployment, especially for local inference, where models are now routinely served at 2-3 bits per parameter. The state of the art is currently split into simple scalar quantization techniques, such as GPTQ or AWQ, which are widely deployed but plateau in accuracy at 3-4 bits per parameter (bpp), and "second-generation" vector- or trellis-quantized methods, such as QTIP, GPTVQ and AQLM, which push the accuracy frontier but are notoriously hard to implement and to scale. We answer in the affirmative, by introducing GSQ (Gumbel-Softmax Quantization), a post-training scalar quantization method which jointly learns the per-coordinate grid assignments and the per-group scales using a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation of the discrete grid. GSQ matches the cardinality of the relaxation to the small number of levels available in the target bit-width regime (e.g., 3-8 levels for ternary and 3 bpp, respectively), making optimization tractable. Practically, on the standard Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct models, GSQ closes most of the gap between scalar quantization and the QTIP frontier at 2 and 3 bits, while using a symmetric scalar grid with group-wise quantization, and thus remains compatible with existing scalar inference kernels. We further show that the same discrete-assignment optimization can be applied to practical GGUF K-Quant checkpoints: starting from publicly released GGUF models, GSQ improves accuracy while projecting the result back into the same deployment format. Finally, GSQ scales to trillion-scale Mixture-of-Experts models such as Kimi-K2.5, where vector-quantized methods are difficult to apply. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: AnyMo: Geometry-Aware Setup-Agnostic Modeling of Human Motion in the Wild
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: As wearable and mobile devices become increasingly embedded in daily life, they offer a practical way to continuously sense human motion in the wild. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: StakeBench: Evaluating Language Understanding Grounded in Market Commitment

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Linear-time Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding with Reference Aggregation

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Examining the Impact of Data and Training Methods on Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Post-training a language model can induce surprising behavioral changes far beyond the intended training target. We examine how the training data, evaluation data, and training method shape where and how strongly misalignment transfers between data and models. We find that EM transfers more strongly to prompts that share the task of the fine-tuning data than to prompts that share its domain. Misalignment transfers even under on-policy distillation, more strongly than under SFT and at a level comparable to off-policy distillation. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Can AI Agents Synthesize Scientific Conclusions in Health?
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Scientific AI agents increasingly retrieve evidence, reason across sources, and synthesize conclusions used in consequential decisions. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Evaluating Compositional Generalization in Transformers: The Role of Composition Equivalence and Module Coverage
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Compositional generalization is an important form of out-of-distribution generalization, defined as the ability to train on some combinations of modules (e.g., functions such as sort, filter) and then generalize to unseen combinations. Despite substantial empirical work evaluating compositional generalization in transformers, findings have been inconsistent because evaluations were often conducted on a limited set of train-test splits, defined in an ad hoc manner. Through a systematic evaluation, we identify two key aspects of the train-test distribution that strongly affect performance: composition equivalence and module coverage. We show that the apparent performance of direct models (trained only on final outputs) results primarily from exploiting composition equivalences, meaning different sequences of modules that reduce to identical end-to-end functions. When benchmarks eliminate these equivalences, performance drops significantly, showing their inability to generalize to compositions of known modules that produce novel end-to-end functions. We further demonstrate that performance degrades monotonically as module coverage shifts increase (when modules appear in different contexts between train and test), affecting both direct and step-by-step models (trained on intermediate and final outputs). These findings have concrete implications for benchmark design: benchmarks that include compositional equivalences can lead to significant overestimation of the generalization abilities of direct models, and benchmarks that include both module coverage violations and compositional equivalences can exacerbate shortcut learning. As a case study, we demonstrate the role of compositional equivalence on the generalization performance of the pre-trained model Llama3-8B on the code-output prediction task in the coding benchmark LiveCodeBench.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Leveraging Psychophysical Attentional Distribution for Gaze-Augmented Reward Modeling
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Integrating human feedback into language models has gained increasing attention as a means to align model outputs with human preferences, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) serving as a prominent framework for preference-based alignment. Recent studies have incorporated eye-tracking (ET) data as an additional supervisory signal for reward model training, grounding reward learning in human reading behavior. Building on this approach, we extend prior fixation-centric models by leveraging established findings from cognitive psychology on human letter recognition. Specifically, we model visual attention as a spatially graded distribution centered on the current gaze location and incorporate this representation into reward model training. Our results show that the reward model trained with the proposed gaze distribution achieves higher preference prediction accuracy than a baseline model. Moreover, some results from our experiments are qualitatively consistent with established findings on human attention during reading, suggesting that they potentially capture cognitively meaningful aspects of human attention allocation.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Prompt-Activation Duality: Improving Activation Steering via Attention-Level Interventions
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Activation steering controls language model behavior by adding directions to internal representations at inference time, but standard residual-stream steering can fail in stateful dialogue. We identify KV-cache contamination as a key failure mode: steered token states are stored and repeatedly reused, turning a local perturbation into cumulative coherence degradation. To address this challenge, we propose Gated Cropped Attention-Delta steering (GCAD), which extracts steering signals from system-prompt contributions to self-attention and applies them with token-level gating. Across persona-steering experiments, GCAD preserves trait control while substantially improving long-horizon coherence. On the main multi-turn benchmark, GCAD improves average coherence drift from -18.6 to -1.9 and raises turn-10 trait expression from 78.0 to 93.1. These results suggest that activation steering becomes more reliable when interventions follow the prompt-mediated pathways that models already use for behavioral control.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared with the verifier's pooled 87.6% (paired difference: +4.8 points, 95% interval [-8.2, 18.5]). A diagnostic sample reveals a distinct failure mode: 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction without ever reaching a judge. Finally, external-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%, compared with 87.6% answer-key match. These audits lack human or formal-kernel ground truth. Open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement, which measures consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth. These results motivate separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity. NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Visual Instruction Tuning Aligns Modalities through Abstraction
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Visual instruction tuning effectively adapts a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) to process image information alongside text. Yet it remains unclear how visual features are embedded within the layer-wise hierarchy of abstractions in the LLM backbone. Across a diverse set of vision-language architectures, we show that instruction tuning primarily serves as a bridge, embedding visual features directly into the intermediate semantic layers of the LLM, bypassing the early layers devoted to unimodal processing. With probing analyses and causal interventions, we show that these intermediate layers constitute the semantic core of vision-language processing and play a critical role in performance across a broad set of multimodal benchmarks. In addition, by comparing the geometry of semantically equivalent visual and textual representations, we find that fine-tuning extends and strengthens the existing abstraction phase, aligning visual features with pre-existing textual ones. Finally, we confirm the functional role of this localized alignment by restricting fine-tuning to intermediate layers alone: this strategy preserves the performance of full fine-tuning on vision-centric benchmarks while reducing training time. Our results suggest that multimodal integration is a localized phenomenon driven by the repurposing of the internal abstraction engine of the LLM.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. We propose {code explanations to address the mismatch in how LLM explanations are generated versus how they are evaluated: a program explains LLM behavior across a dataset of inputs, and its execution enables automatic verification. We define Consistency metric that measures the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs, and use it to evaluate and select candidate programs. Across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks, we find that LLMs can produce highly consistent code explanations in several settings. Code explanations are also 6$\times$ to 100$\times$ shorter than CoT, and better align with model behavior in 9 out of 24 settings. However, consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where generated programs reproduce model outputs no more frequently than an uninformative explanation baseline, and these programs often rely on longer hard-coded patterns. In experiments with Claude Opus 5.5, providing the model with consistency feedback and code execution improves explanation consistency across tasks, but consistency remains significantly lower on more complex tasks. Our findings establish executable code as a novel, verifiable, and compact approach to explaining LLM behavior and highlight verification feedback as a promising direction for improving explanation consistency. The code for this paper is at https://github.com/rajesh-lab/code-as-explanations.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models to Know What They Know
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Evaluating true metacognition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is difficult due to biases and heuristics. This paper presents a framework to measure and enhance LLM metacognition while controlling for these biases. A measurement method using the $d'_{\rm type2}$ metric is established to isolate metacognitive ability. The Evolution Strategy for Metacognitive Alignment (ESMA) is proposed, demonstrating robust generalization across unseen datasets, languages, and newly acquired knowledge. Gradual parameter updates reveal that these improvements are driven by a sparse set of parameters, opening a potential avenue for targeted metacognitive optimization.

NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.title: MITRA-Swarm: Injecting Explicit Linguistic Structure into Foundation Models for Classical Machine Translation
NLP / Computation and Language (Top Venu.summary: Classical Sanskrit poses three challenges unresolved by single-call monolithic models: morphophonemic fusion Sandhi, dense nominal compounding Samāsa, and discourse-level zero-anaphora forced by poetic meter. We present MITRA-Swarm, a multi-agent architecture injecting explicit linguistic structure into an otherwise monolithic pipeline: a Sandhi-splitting agent, a parallel array of generalist gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and domain-specialized gemma-2-mitra-it translators, and a discourse-aware Ellipsis Restorer that consults corpus-derived register tags to avoid inventing active-voice subjects in impersonal legal and philosophical registers. Two separated judges evaluate quality: a routing judge ($J_{\text{route}}$, same model family as the generators) driving an internal critique loop, and an independent reporting judge ($J_{\text{report}}=$gpt-4o-mini, no shared vendor lineage) scoring every output exactly once. On a stratified benchmark of 1,000 verses across five registers (23,990 scored verdicts, 12-condition pre-registered ablation), the full swarm reaches $85.90$ MQM against a monolithic baseline of $85.27$ ($Δ=+0.63$, $p_{\text{adj}}=0.0018$, 95% CI $[+0.30,+0.97]$), and isolated discourse restoration alone accounts for $+0.44$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$), outperforming a call-count-matched self-refinement baseline by $+0.51$ MQM ($p_{\text{adj}}=0.0288$). Severe per-verse failures (MQM$<80$) fall from $9.0\%$ to $7.6\%$, at roughly $9\times$ the per-verse inference cost of the baseline. Additionally, $J_{\text{route}}$ scores its own family's outputs $2$-$7$ MQM higher than $J_{\text{report}}$ on every one of the 12 conditions, empirically motivating the two-judge split; and a preflight screen of a 192,151-entry retrieval index against all 12 evaluation works verifies 0 reference leaks across 269 runtime checks. These are small gains on a metric saturating near 85-86.

Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.title: Controllable and Content-Based Recommendations
Information Retrieval (Top Venues & Labs.summary: Traditional recommendation systems rely on latent (dense) representations, making them difficult to interpret and control. We propose the Controllable and Content-Based Recommendations (CCBR) framework, which builds its recommendations from textual user profile representations. CCBR plugs into collaborative filtering models and introduces controllability via text bottlenecks. We show that CCBR enables text-based and multimodal interventions, allowing users to steer the model towards the directions they prefer. Different from existing controllable recommendation systems, CCBR infers the text summaries directly from item contents (images, audio or video). Across image, audio, and video datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed framework obtains competitive model performance with standard (latent-representation) models while providing controllable model summaries via text. The model also outperforms TEARS, a recent baseline for controllable recommendation systems. Through systematic interventions, we demonstrate the efficacy of the steering mechanism.

Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
Multiagent Systems (Top Venues & Labs).summary: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

Databases (Core).title: Separations Between Submodular-Like Graph Widths
Databases (Core).summary:
Many algorithmic frameworks exist for evaluating join queries. They range from simple ones, such as dynamic programming over a single tree decomposition, high-degree-low-degree splitting from graph algorithms, and the degree uniformization of Joglekar and Ré, to sophisticated ones based on information-theoretic inequalities, such as the PANDA framework for submodular width. Each of these frameworks except high-degree-low-degree splitting comes with a width notion of the query that determines its running-time exponent. We fill this gap by formalizing high-degree-low-degree splitting with $\ell$ degree classes, which gives rise to the degree-splitting width $\mathrm{ds}_\ell$-width. These width notions form a hierarchy, but it was not known whether the more complicated frameworks achieve better worst-case exponents than the simpler ones on any graph query.
  We study this question for full self-join-free join queries with binary relations, which amounts to colored subgraph isomorphism for a pattern graph $H$. We show that every inequality in the hierarchy $\mathrm{subw} \le \#\mathrm{subw} \le \text{m-width} \le \mathrm{ds}_\ell\text{-width}$ can be strict. For instance, $\text{m-width}(K_{3,3}) = 2 < \mathrm{ds}_\ell\text{-width}(K_{3,3})$ for every constant $\ell$, so no constant number of degree classes reaches the exponent of degree uniformization. We find the smallest separating patterns, with 8, 9, and 6 nodes, respectively, by an exhaustive search with a software tool that computes these widths via mixed integer linear programming. Along the way, we give a degree-based algorithm that removes the polylogarithmic overhead of degree uniformization when evaluating full join queries. Furthermore, we show that with logarithmically many degree classes, the degree-splitting width coincides with the m-width of Joglekar and Ré. Finally, we discuss several open problems.

Databases (Core).title: PLDP-IDS: Personalized Local Differential Privacy for Infinite Data Stream
Databases (Core).summary: Existing $w$-event local differential privacy (LDP) mechanisms for streaming data impose a uniform privacy window and budget, forcing all users to adopt the most stringent privacy requirement. We study personalized continual frequency estimation under LDP, where each user specifies her own window size and privacy budget, and identify two challenges. First, a single sampling size cannot balance sampling and perturbation errors for privacy groups with heterogeneous requirements. Second, borrowing estimates from groups with larger budgets reduces variance but introduces bias when privacy preferences correlate with the data. We first propose Optimal Population Selection (OPS) and two OPS-guided mechanisms, PLPD and PLPA, which use one privacy-compatible sampling size for all users. Since one size cannot fit all groups and pooling their estimates is biased under privacy--data correlation, we further develop PLPD$^+$ and PLPA$^+$, which combine group-aware population scheduling with bias-aware cross-group fusion while preserving personalized $w$-event LDP. Experiments on real-world and synthetic streams show that, compared with the direct personalized extension of LDP-IDS, PLPA$^+$ reduces the average mean squared error (AMSE) by 52.3\% and 40.8\% on average, respectively, and remains 4.3--5.1$\times$ more accurate than PLPA under strong privacy--data correlation.

Databases (Core).title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
Databases (Core).summary:
As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle.
  We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not.
  On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

Databases (Core).title: FlinkEval: A Synthetic Corpus for Evaluating Natural Language Interfaces to Streaming SQL
Databases (Core).summary: Existing natural-language-to-SQL benchmarks primarily evaluate queries over bounded relational data, leaving streaming semantics underexplored. We introduce FlinkEval, an execution-grounded synthetic benchmark comprising 3,903 question--SQL pairs across 45 industry domains and 45 semantic labels. We create diverse schemas and domain-plausible, temporally consistent data through iterative generation and validation. SQL patterns collected from the human-written NL2SQL pairs and vendor documentation drive quota-balanced generation, and execution with a repair loop on Confluent Cloud Apache Flink produces reference queries covering windowing, temporal joins, pattern matching, nested types, and data manipulation. The corpus includes paired schema-explicit and business-language requests, with annotations for analysis by query pattern, complexity, and execution mode. A seven-level Question Specification Ladder examines semantics-preserving reformulation and underspecified requests augmented with oracle-derived clues. Baseline evaluations combine execution outcomes with adjudicated LLM judgments, revealing challenges in pattern composition and request specification.

Databases (Core).title: Community Search under Member-Specific Tolerances
Databases (Core).summary: We study community search when each member has its own tolerance for differences in position, as when members of a group interact repeatedly and influence one another. A latitude-consistent community (LCC) contains the query vertex, is connected, has minimum degree at least k, and bounds its diameter by the smallest member tolerance. The bound is exactly the condition under which every interaction in a connected closed group stays accepted under bounded-confidence dynamics for every choice of positive weights. It also prevents rejection under social-judgment dynamics, whereas the pairwise condition and other natural relaxations preserve neither guarantee. Finding a maximum LCC is NP-hard even in the plane, and with unbounded dimension, deciding whether an LCC exists is NP-complete for every fixed k>=2. LatSweep fixes the answer's smallest tolerance and turns the coupled bound into a best-first sweep over candidate thresholds, yielding an exact branch-and-bound algorithm, a (1,2)-bicriteria approximation and two feasible heuristics. Across eight graphs with up to 1.8 billion edges, six with synthetic positions and tolerances, the exact algorithm proves optimality on all but 9 of 3,700 efficiency queries; in a shared implementation on two large graphs, its branch-and-bound solver proves more queries than a reimplemented maximum-(k,r)-core algorithm, a mixed-integer program and CP-SAT. In simulations of closed groups, LCC groups keep every accepted interaction under uneven influence, whereas 3-40% of pairwise-compatible groups lose some. On three location-based networks, tolerance-agnostic groups often place another member's home beyond a member's estimated travel radius. Enforcing every member's tolerance causes no measurable loss of co-visits relative to spatial communities of the same size. Relative to the larger pairwise-compatible groups, it can cause a size-adjusted loss.
